Eubanks suffers torn pectoral muscle
New York Knicks reserve center Drew Eubanks has a torn pectoral muscle and will be sidelined for an extended period of time, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania. The Knicks will waive Eubanks, who was competing for a roster spot.

Goodwill: Pistons inquired about trades for Durant, Leonard
ESPN reporter Vincent Goodwill wrote Friday about why the Detroit Pistons and big man Jalen Duren -- who engaged in a contract stalemate this offseason before Duren got a five-year, $200 million contract -- needed each other. In that piece, Goodwill dropped a nugget on other players Detroit explored adding since its season ended:

The Pistons inquired about trading for Kawhi Leonard and Kevin Durant this offseason, according to league sources, and were positioned to offer Austin Reaves a big free agent contract if the Los Angeles Lakers opened the door. None of that materialized.
The Pistons had heard Leonard wasn't interested in coming to Detroit amid the Clippers' cap-circumvention scandal, per league sources, and the Rockets weren't willing to engage on Durant despite the close relationship he shares with Cunningham. As for Reaves, once the Lakers blew him away with a max contract offer, he wasn't going anywhere -- he'd already turned down being drafted by Detroit under the Troy Weaver era to go the undrafted route and sign with the Lakers a few years ago.

The ramifications of the Hukporti injury for Philadelphia
The season ending Achilles injury to Ariel Hukporti has roster ramifications for the 76ers.

Philadelphia is $1.8 million below the first apron, so they are not allowed to sign a player with their open roster spot until Dec. 4. The 76ers could create financial flexibility but at the cost of Jabari Walker, whose $2.6 million salary is guaranteed for only $250,000. Walker scored 11 points and grabbed 11 rebounds in their pre-season opener.

The 76ers do have an open two-way spot and can sign a player with three years or less in service.

Beyond starter Joel Embiid, Philadelphia's frontcourt depth is Dean Wade, Adem Bona, Dominick Barlow and Walker. -- Bobby Marks

Charania: Hukporti sustained a season-ending ruptured Achilles
An MRI confirm Tuesday that Philadelphia 76ers' center Ariel Hukporti sustained a season-ending torn right Achilles, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania. Hukporti will undergo surgery for the injury later today.

Doncic, who 'worked his butt off all summer,' lights up Kings
A lighter Luka Doncic scored an easy 21 first-half points in the Los Angeles Lakers' preseason opener over the Sacramento Kings on Monday night, needing only 16 minutes to sharpen up his game in a 127-103 blowout in Sacramento.
Doncic was listed at 244 pounds prior to the 2025-26 season. That dipped to 230 pounds entering training camp. The difference in physique from his heavier days is obvious.

"The guy worked his butt off all summer staying in shape and actually ran this summer," coach JJ Redick said. "He actually did like sprints and stuff. Came into camp in fantastic shape."

The Lakers were without Austin Reaves and Walker Kessler in the preseason opener. Reaves tweaked his ankle recently, and Kessler jammed a finger on the backboard. Both are listed as day-to-day. Without either, the Lakers still rolled through the Kings. Doncic scored all 21 of his points in a 73-point Lakers first half, resting while the backups finished the job. He made three 3s, four shots in the paint and got to the line for nine free throws.

"For someone who normally plays a ton of live basketball [in the summer], he didn't do as much of that by design," Redick said. "We've seen him literally every day in camp incrementally get more and more in rhythm."

Doncic badly strained his hamstring in early April and missed the entire Lakers playoff run while rehabbing the injury. He said he felt "great" against the Kings but downplayed any larger changes to his training regimen.

"I feel probably a little more rested," Doncic said. "I didn't play [on the Slovenian] national team." -- Anthony Slater

Hawkins, Grizzlies mutually agree to part ways
The Memphis Grizzlies and guard Jordan Hawkins have agreed to part ways via waivers, allowing the 2023 lottery pick to find a new home in free agency, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania.

The move comes three weeks after arriving as part of a four-player trade with the New Orleans Pelicans for AJ Johnson and Taj Gibson.

Hawkins, 24, averaged 5.1 points in 51 games last season and struggled to find consistent playing time in New Orleans' crowded backcourt rotation. The former UConn star played just 13.6 minutes per game, a significant decrease from the 2024-25 season, when he played 23.6 minutes per game and averaged 10.8 points per game.

Mitch Johnson excited about Billy Donovan's role with Spurs
San Antonio Spurs coach Mitch Johnson likes what he's seen so far at training camp from new lead assistant coach Billy Donovan.

"I don't want to be naive enough to think I'm going to tell you what a 61-year old Hall of Fame coach like Billy Donovan and his resume can bring to the table," Johnson said. "I'm excited he's here. He's a tremendous person, great personality, fits in seamlessly. He's got worlds of experience and he's an extremely hard worker. He's not kicking up his feet and telling stories. He's rolling his sleeves up and getting his hands dirty. He's going to help all of us and probably me, specifically, a ton this year."

Donovan joined the staff in July, replacing former lead assistant Sean Sweeney, who left San Antonio to take the head coaching job in Orlando. Sweeney ran the Spurs' defense last season, helping it improve from 25th to third in the NBA in defensive rating (110.4).

Donovan won't be tasked with taking on Sweeney's responsibilities, according to sources, however. San Antonio brought in Donovan to lean on his experience on both ends of the floor, as well as his vast knowledge of the NBA and college games.

A member of the Naismith Basketball Hall of Fame class of 2025, Donovan joined the Spurs after 11 seasons as an NBA coach with the Chicago Bulls and Oklahoma City Thunder, after capturing two college basketball national titles in 2006 and 2007 with the Florida Gators. -- Michael C. Wright

Embiid "full participant" in first Sixers' practice
Joel Embiid was a "full participant all the way through" for the Philadelphia 76ers first practice of training camp, Sixers coach Nick Nurse said Tuesday.

"He looked great," Nurse said of Embiid. "Very, very good news from the standpoint of where it's been the last couple years, last couple summers leading into today. ... It's great to see."

After being named the league MVP in 2023, the 32-year-old center has missed 150 games over the last three seasons because of various injuries.

He also sat out four of the Sixers' 11 playoff games in the spring because of appendicitis, right hip soreness and a right ankle sprain.

The only Sixers player who did not participate in Tuesday's practice according to a team spokesperson was backup big man Adem Bona, who is dealing with a sprained left foot.

Anfernee Simons, who signed a two-year, $12.3 million contract to join Philadelphia in July, said Embiid's presence in the gym was already notable leading up to the start of camp.

"Everybody's been impressed around here about how he's come in and worked," Simons said. "Joel is going to be Joel. He's going to be a dominant player always. We just want to continue for him to be himself, as well, and I think everybody's going to be able to work around that."

Despite the injuries, the 10-year veteran still averaged 26.9 points, 7.7 rebounds, 3.9 assists and 1.2 blocks per game last season.

Embiid's inclusion only added to what several Sixers players described as an "exciting" opening day with LeBron James and Jaylen Brown completing their first official practice with the franchise.

"With any team, we got to start somewhere, and then we got to get better and better, and just keep trying to reach our ceiling, right?" Nurse said. "That happens day-to-day. Can we get up tomorrow, like, 98% as excited as we did today? It's going to be hard to get as excited as we all were today, right?

"But we need to come back, and we need to keep climbing that mountain. That's a daily process. I just want them to reach their potential. If they do, great things are going to happen." -- Dave McMenamin

Bronny on LeBron James' Lakers exit: 'He's got his own path'

Sept. 28

Bronny on LeBron James' Lakers exit: 'He's got his own path'

When LeBron James chose to leave the Los Angeles Lakers in free agency over the summer, he consulted his family on the decision to sign with the Philadelphia 76ers. But when it came to his son/teammate Bronny, much was apparently left unsaid.

"We're men of very little words when it comes to talking about business and what we're going to do and how we feel about each other. So it wasn't really much [discussion] to be honest with you," Bronny James said Monday at Lakers media day.

"He's got his own path and I got my own. He knows that I want to make a name for myself and I want to continue my career and keep growing as a player. And he knows that I want to focus on that. So he decided to do that."

LeBron and Bronny have routinely been in unique situations in league history, whether it was opening night two years ago, when the father and son entered the game together, or last year in the playoffs, where they combined to deliver a 10-0 run during a victory over the Houston Rockets. Navigating a complex free agency in which the father leaves and the son stays is another one for the books.

Tatum 'comfortable' leading new-look Celtics post-Brown trade

Jayson Tatum's one constant during his development into a star with the Boston Celtics was having Jaylen Brown as a teammate.

That partnership ended this offseason when the Celtics' front office decided to trade Brown -- the 2024 NBA Finals MVP -- to the Philadelphia 76ers in what was largely a cost-cutting move that broke up the duo most responsible for leading Boston to the 2024 NBA championship.

"The business of the NBA comes and plays a part at some point. And I've seen it in my almost 10 years in this league," Tatum said during Celtics media day on Monday. "For me it's more so being grateful for what we accomplished and what he means for this city and to this organization. Just the ups and downs in our career that we were able to grow and learn from and made us the players that we are today. So really just being thankful for those nine years."

Suns owner Ishbia says mortgage company woes won't hurt team
It's well-known at this point that billionaire Mat Ishbia's mortgage company has had a rough financial stretch.

The owner of the Phoenix Suns said Monday that will have "zero" effect on his spending habits when it comes to basketball. In fact, the 46-year-old said he's working on purchasing 14% more of the team, bringing his total to roughly 80%.

Ishbia's company -- United Wholesale Mortgage -- suffered a reported $450 million net loss in the second quarter this year, calling into question if the sizable dip would affect his basketball business. The outspoken Ishbia was adamant that nothing would change for the NBA franchise when it comes to spending on players or the fan experience.

Williamson not where he wants to be
New Orleans Pelicans forward Zion Williamson kept his answer brief when asked how he would summarize his first seven years as an NBA player.
"I'm not where I want to be," said Williamson, whom the Pelicans drafted with the No. 1 pick out of Duke in 2019. "I'm not where I need to be."

Butler indicates he is 'ahead' in his knee rehab

Nearing the eight-month mark since his right ACL surgery, Jimmy Butler III is hesitant to put a specific target date on his eventual NBA return, but he did express optimism in advance of Golden State Warriors training camp.

"I promise you I'm coming back, and it's going to be -- I think it's going to be, like, real eye-popping for everybody how I'm still going to be nice," Butler said. "Probably nicer, honestly."

Butler has only recently advanced to running, and he will be limited to light on-court individual work when the team begins practice in Hawaii on Tuesday afternoon.

It will be several weeks before Butler is expected to advance to a more rigorous stage of his rehab, and the team's lead medical decision-maker, Rick Celebrini, is known for his cautiousness in the later stages of the rehab process.

A January or February return can be considered on the optimistic side for Butler, who turned 37 earlier this month. But Butler did say that the strengthening tests on the knee indicate he is ahead of schedule.

"My numbers are staggering," Butler said. "They're off the charts. I'm ahead, so they say. So, I just know that all the work that I've been doing, whether it be at home, in L.A., in Europe, in South America, wherever the case may be, I've been doing all the right things. So, I am confident that whenever I come back, I'll be more than ready, I'll be more than healthy and I'll be a better all-around player than I was whenever I went down." -- Anthony Slater

Pistons eye "better version" of Cunningham

Detroit Pistons coach J.B. Bickerstaff has held many offseason conversations with All-NBA guard Cade Cunningham about seizing greatness and the necessary steps toward improving after last year's playoff run that stretched to Game 7 of the Eastern Conference semifinals.

Bickerstaff has guaranteed "a better version" Cunningham this season, which could be a scary sight after he averaged 23.9 points, 9.9 assists, 5.5 rebounds and 1.4 steals in 33.9 minutes during 2025-26. But Cunningham also led the East in turnovers per game after finishing with the second most in 2024-25.

"I don't have to challenge Cade, and that's why he is who he is," Bickerstaff said. "Because he's pulling. He's not being pushed."

Cunningham showed up in a fresh pair of Nike S.T. Charge "Detroit Tough" sneakers in Pistons colors. He will also receive his own signature Nike shoe, which is expected to debut during the second half of the season.

"I'm thankful to be in these shoes. I'm thankful to have the opportunity to represent my family in this way," Cunningham said. "Represent where I come from, but then to represent the city of Detroit.

"In a city like this, it's a blessing. I'm thankful for it, I don't take it for granted and I'm trying to make the most out of it." -- Eric Woodyard

Hornets waive former No. 8 pick Dillingham

The Charlotte Hornets are waiving guard Rob Dillingham, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania. Dillingham was traded from the Chicago Bulls on Saturday for Buddy Hield and cash. The Hornets created a $9.6 million trade exception with the move.

Dillingham, 21, appeared in 30 games for the Bulls last season, averaging 9.6 points and 2.8 assists.

SGA on chance at historic third straight MVP

At Oklahoma City Thunder media day, guard Shai Gilgeous-Alexander discussed the possibility of winning a third straight NBA MVP award and whether that's something he ponders going into this season.

"No different than any other year: Try to be the best player I can be, try to implement the things I just worked on," Gilgeous-Alexander said.

"The decision for MVP is literally 82 games away. I'm not going to win the award in the first week of the season. ... That kind of recipe for me in the past has kind of worked, and I've been fortunate to win two in a row.

"We need to be laser focused on ourselves. We need to take the lessons from that [Western Conference finals] series, for sure, and we did. But it's certainly not something that we overcorrect for, because you end up chasing your shadow, and it prevents you from being your best as you move forward."

ESPN's Summer Forecast gave Gilgeous-Alexander the fourth-best chance at the 2027 MVP, behind Victor Wembanyama, Nikola Jokic and Luka Doncic. No player has won three consecutive MVPs since Larry Bird in 1984, 1985 and 1986. -- Baxter Holmes

Doncic talks LeBron exit, Lakers "championship" ceiling
Speaking to ESPN's Brian Windhorst during Los Angeles Lakers media day, guard Luka Doncic detailed his reaction to LeBron James leaving for the Philadelphia 76ers this past summer and why he thinks a successful 2026-27 includes a Lakers run to the title:

"It was kind of sad. Playing with LeBron was amazing. There's a lot of things I learned from him. ... We all know who LeBron James is."

Shams: Duren's relationship with Pistons "has fractures"

Simmons "didn't touch a ball for a year"

During Sacramento Kings media day, guard Ben Simmons laid out the reasons he chose the Kings and why he's excited for the 2026-27 season.

"The expectations are low. I feel like that's been something on me too, so we can relate in that way," Simmons told reporters. "I think we have a chip on our shoulder."

Simmons last played in 2024-25, appearing in 51 games for the Brooklyn Nets and LA Clippers. The three-time All-Star said the time away gave him the chance to focus on "getting my body right and my mind right."

Pistons GM hasn't spoken with Duren all summer

Jalen Duren and the Detroit Pistons have a decision to make as the clock ticks closer to Oct. 1 -- the deadline to sign a one-year, $9.6 million qualifying offer.

For Duren, he can accept the five-year, $200 million contract that has been offered by Detroit or he can become the first player named All-NBA or All-Star to sign the qualifying offer. If he chooses the latter, Duren will hold veto power on any trade this season and be an unrestricted free agent next summer.

For the Pistons, weighing the risk of having an All-NBA player on a one-year contract and, more importantly, the likelihood he will depart next summer as a free agent is key.

There are eight projected teams that have significant cap space to sign Duren to a four-year, $189 million max contract.

"I can't control the different things that he does or his group does," Pistons president of basketball operations Trajan Langdon said at media day. "For me, it's control what we can and letting him know he is a big part of what we do."

Langdon also said he hasn't spoken with Duren all summer during Pistons media day. -- Bobby Marks

Mitchell: LeBron to Cavs made sense "for a lot of reasons"

At Cavaliers media day, Donovan Mitchell said that in his mind, he thought LeBron James would return to Cleveland because "for a lot of reasons it made sense."

"I didn't think Philly. I thought if he didn't come here, it'd be Golden State," Mitchell said.

After being swept in the Eastern Conference finals by the eventual champion New York Knicks then missing out on James in free agency, Cleveland kept its core intact. The Cavs signed Mitchell to a four-year, $273 million maximum extension and re-signed James Harden to a three-year, $97 million contract. Cleveland did make one major addition by acquiring Peyton Watson from the Denver Nuggets in a multiteam trade then signing the restricted free agent to a four-year, $88 million deal.

Speaking for the first time since their extensions, Mitchell and Harden both said their approaches to their new deals -- Mitchell signing as soon as he was eligible with Harden opting out to give Cleveland more flexibility to make moves -- reflected a team-first mindset.

"This is something that I want to do, and I want to win a championship," Harden said. "So, what does that look like? Making the team better, making the team whole to where we give ourselves a chance. By the way, you can have the best talented team, which I've been on before, and still not win.

"We waited, waited, waited until the front office called me, made sure that we got everything that we can get, and then we signed. We got a long way to go, but I love the direction and steps that we're taking here as a unit from top to bottom." -- Daniel Oyefusi

MacMahon: Thunder adjusting to roster changes
The departures of three championship-winning teammates doesn't yet feel like reality for Thunder superstar Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, who kidded that he still expected Luguentz Dort, Isaiah Joe and Aaron Wiggins to show up for Oklahoma City's team picture Monday afternoon.

"It's the business of the NBA, right?" Gilgeous-Alexander said, referring to the series of financially motivated trades. "I don't think anybody has played with all 12 guys their whole career. It sucks a little bit.

"My mind never even went to what we were going to be like on the court. It was more like the brotherhood."

As fellow OKC guard Jalen Williams added, "It's the weirdest thing ever." -- Tim MacMahon

Clippers announce Ingram has partially torn Achilles

The LA Clippers announced they found a partially torn Achilles tendon in Brandon Ingram's foot after his recent heel surgery. He will miss the start of the 2026-27 season.

Jokic: "I'm gonna sign next year"

Denver Nuggets center Nikola Jokic reiterated his commitment to the franchise at Monday's media day.

"I'm gonna sign next year," Jokic said. "If they want me."

Curry said knee is ready to go for the season

Golden State Warriors superstar guard Stephen Curry addressed the media Monday in offering positive updates on his injured knee.

"Knee's feeling great. Ready to go. No issues," Curry said. "I feel a lot stronger and understanding of what I'm dealing with."

Curry did acknowledge a "management element" but said there are currently no restrictions.

Nuggets confident in Jokic's future with franchise

Members of the Denver Nuggets' front office, general manager Jon Wallace and executive vice president of basketball Ben Tenzer addressed the media on Monday and answered questions regarding Nikola Jokic's future with the franchise. The three-time MVP didn't sign an extension this offseason.

"We feel very comfortable with the relation and trust there," Tenzer said. "We have no concerns."

LeBron: I wanted to finish my career with the Knicks
New Philadelphia 76er LeBron James said his decision came down to five teams this offseason and that he envisioned going to the New York Knicks before they won the 2026 title.

"I had visions of playing in [Madison Square] Garden and finishing my career in the Garden," James told ESPN on Monday during the 76ers' media day. "One of the best places I've ever played.

"I think it's the No. 1 arena in the world, as far as for a basketball player. But after they beat San Antonio, I was like, 'Hey, I can't.' I couldn't do it."

James and the 76ers will play the Knicks at the Garden on opening night, Oct. 20.

No update on Gary Trent Jr. investigation

Milwaukee Bucks governor Wes Edens did not provide an update on the league investigation into Gary Trent Jr.'s contract.

"I don't have any update," Edens said. "We're working with the league and fully cooperating with them. But I don't have any insight beyond that."

The NBA is looking into a potential cap-circumvention violation by the Bucks around Trent's deal this offseason.

Cronin: Blazers have "belief" in Ja Morant
Portland Trail Blazers' general manager Joe Cronin addressed why the franchise decided to trade for Ja Morant this offseason during Portland's media day on Monday.

"Just straight belief in Ja," Cronin said. "Our view of Ja as still a very high-level player.

"I'm sure there will be questions about fit, but we're very focused on talent."

Cronin also said veteran guard Jrue Holiday could play some minutes on the wing for Portland this season, while adding that Holiday and veteran guard Damian Lillard will have a positive influence on Morant.

Kerr: Rookie Lendeborg going to "play a ton"

Golden State Warriors coach Steve Kerr said during Monday's media day that he expects rookie Yaxel Lendeborg to "play a ton" this season.

"He's clearly going to play a ton," Kerr said. "He gives us the size and the versatility that we need.

"Whether he's a starter or coming off the bench, that will be determined the next couple of weeks."

Lendeborg was the No. 11 pick in the 2026 NBA draft and averaged 15.1 points per game at Michigan last season.

Embiid: 'Extremely excited' about this year's team
Philadelphia 76ers center Joel Embiid said Monday that he feels like the team finally has the right mix of players, after an offseason in which the franchise traded for Jaylen Brown and signed LeBron James to join the young guard tandem of VJ Edgecombe and Tyrese Maxey.

"It's hard to win when you get a group of guys together for one year, two years, maybe," he said. "I'm extremely excited about this team because we have the right mix of veteran leadership and younger guys. We might have some ups and downs, but we're gonna get there."

Wembanyama addresses last year's Finals loss
After leading by double digits in each of the five games in last season's NBA Finals, San Antonio Spurs center Victor Wembanyama said his memories of it will fuel the team this season.

"I couldn't imagine a better motivation," he said.

Harper addresses role for coming season
After offseason chatter about his role, San Antonio Spurs guard Dylan Harper said he'd follow the coaches' lead this season.

"Everyone has a competitive edge to them. But the biggest thing for me is whatever I can do, just like last year, to help the team win," he said. "Whatever position the coaches think is best for me to be in, that's the position I'll happily go in."

First look at LeBron in a 76ers uniform
New Philadelphia 76ers forward LeBron James is taking questions from reporters on Monday. Here's what he had to say when asked about his initial impressions of his team:

"Everybody is on the same page," James said. "We are all speaking the same language."

LeBron addressed his role too, saying he's open to whatever the team needs from him to win.

"Whatever they need me to do," he said. "The luxury of my game is I can do everything. ... Literally, I can do everything"

Kawhi: I was a distraction, ready to move forward
In his first public appearance with the Toronto Raptors after a controversy-filled summer, Kawhi Leonard addressed the NBA's investigation into him and his business dealings.

"I know why some of you guys came. You want to hear about the investigation. But in talking with the NBA and PA, I think the best decision is to move forward and focus on my time being a Toronto Raptor," he said. "I already was a distraction for the past 70 days and wasn't able to meet my teammates or do any of that stuff, minicamp stuff, so, moving forward, I just want to talk about the Toronto Raptors."

Haliburton: I am 100% healthy
Indiana Pacers guard Tyrese Haliburton said Monday that he is healthy and ready for the season.

"I am healthy. I am 100%," he said. "There will be no restrictions. That is not news. There is no source. I am the source. I am ready to go for the year."

Porzingis out indefinitely in blow to Warriors
Golden State Warriors big man Kristaps Porzingis is out indefinitely to open training camp with a health issue, according to the team.
In late July, Porzingis agreed to a two-year, $40 million contract with a player option on the second season to return to the Warriors.

Brown: KAT, Hart extension talks won't be a distraction
After reports surfaced last week that negotiations between the New York Knicks and center Karl-Anthony Towns had hit a stalemate, coach Mike Brown said Monday neither Towns' situation nor Hart's would linger in the locker room.

"We talk about everything [with the team]," Brown said. "We don't want to have any elephants in the room."

"I'm not involved in it. They'll figure it out. Control what you can control."

And here's what Towns said about a potential extension: "I've made it known I want to play here. Been a fan since I was a kid. I'd like to get it done."

Hornets GM: Brandon Miller to be ready for training camp
After undergoing offseason surgery on his left shoulder, Hornets wing Brandon Miller should be a full participant in training camp and "ready to roll" for opening night, Hornets general manager Jeff Peterson said Monday.

Miller, 23, is entering his fourth NBA season after being the No. 2 pick in the 2023 draft.

Duren won't be at Pistons media day, start of camp
Detroit Pistons All-Star center Jalen Duren is not attending the team's media day on Monday or the start of training camp as his contract standoff continues, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania on Monday.

Duren, a restricted free agent, is declining the team's five-year, $200 million fully guaranteed offer as both sides remain at a stalemate ahead of the Thursday deadline on a one-year, $9.6 million qualifying offer, sources said.

Sept. 26

Bulls trade Dillingham to Hornets for Hield, cash
The Chicago Bulls and Charlotte Hornets agreed to a trade sending Rob Dillingham to Charlotte for Buddy Hield and cash, the teams announced Saturday.

2026 NBA offseason trade grades

Sept. 25

What's next for Curry and the Warriors?
Stephen Curry's two-year, $116 million extension made him the first player in NBA history to amass $600 million in career on-court earnings.

The deal has also put the Golden State Warriors in position to have extra spending power next summer.

By Curry taking $10 million less than the maximum allowed, the Warriors project to have nearly $38 million in cap space in 2027. Golden State could increase its projection to $55 million if center Kristaps Porzingis is waived in the offseason. Porzingis' $20 million salary for next season is guaranteed for $3 million.

For Golden State to have ample room, forwards Draymond Green and Jimmy Butler III would need to sign elsewhere or at a significantly lesser salary. They will be free agents next summer.

Both salary projections include the $17 million free agent hold of guard Brandin Podziemski. The 2023 first-round pick is eligible until Oct. 19 to extend his contract. -- Bobby Marks

Grading the Curry deal: Why Warriors don't get an A

Hornets star Knueppel sidelined by hamstring injury
The Charlotte Hornets announced that Kon Knueppel will be out for at least the entire preseason because of a left hamstring injury.

James: Maxey, Embiid were factors in joining 76ers
LeBron James said his longstanding friendship with All-Star Tyrese Maxey and a desire to help Joel Embiid win his first NBA title played significant roles in his decision to sign a two-year, $8 million contract with the Philadelphia 76ers in July.

"[Embiid has] done everything in our league, and the only thing he has not done is win a championship. And I want to try to help him get that first one," James said. "He has a city on his back. He's been 'The Process' for 10 years, 12 years, however long he's been there. But I think it's time we even get you deeper into the process. And I hope that I can be, kind of, that final little piece that can help him get over the hump."

Grizzlies waive Russell
The Memphis Grizzlies have waived D'Angelo Russell, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania. Russell has made one All-Star team during his career and was selected No. 2 in the 2015 NBA draft.

stories.headline: Every team's odds to win the 2026 World Series: Brewers become clear favorites
stories.summary: Every MLB team's odds to win the 2026 World Series as the playoffs continue.
stories.body:
For the first time in the 2026 MLB season, there is an odds-on favorite for the World Series -- and it's not the Los Angeles Dodgers. After taking a 3-0 lead in the National League Championship Series, the Milwaukee Brewers are the -145 favorites for this season's title after beginning the campaign at a 14th-best 35-1.

The Dodgers, meanwhile, are out to 11-1 for the World Series after being the favorites all season long and coming into the postseason with +200 championship odds. They are also +800 to mount a series comeback that has only been accomplished once in MLB history.

Either Milwaukee or Los Angeles would be favored in the World Series against whichever team comes out of the American League. After dropping Game 1 of the ALCS, the Tampa Bay Rays recovered nicely with a Game 2 win, making them second-favorites for the World Series at +300 and favored to win their series against the Cleveland Guardians at -135. Cleveland lengthened from +400 to +550 for the title following Tuesday's loss.

Odds by DraftKings at time of publication.

stories.headline: Michael 'Venom' Page: UFC's Dana White 'never really a fan of me'
stories.summary: Michael 'Venom' Page has said that his relationship with UFC president Dana White was "non-existent."
stories.body:
Michael "Venom" Page said that his relationship with UFC president Dana White was "nonexistent."

Page joined the UFC in 2023 with his stock at an all-time high after serving as the face of Bellator courtesy of a series of exciting stoppages with his unique freestyle striking style.

But he couldn't replicate that in the UFC with a run of impressive, albeit uninspiring, decision wins in the promotion, along with a solitary defeat to Ian Machado-Garry, leading to the conclusion of his six-fight contract.

White confirmed in September that the UFC would not pursue another deal, and Page announced this week that his next venture is with KSI's Misfits boxing in a "multi-fight, multi-year agreement." And reflecting on his time in the promotion, Page said he felt that White was "never really a fan of me from the beginning."

"Literally nonexistent [relationship with White]," Page told ESPN. "I think we've had a couple of very brief conversations, very, very brief. [Chief business officer Hunter Campbell] was the person that I spoke with quite regularly. I was thankful for him. ... It was him that signed me. It was more Hunter that was the person that was like, 'Look, I want you in the UFC.'

"So I feel like Dana White's never really been a fan of me from the beginning, or I think it came from somebody else. And because I also didn't deliver it in the way he wanted me to deliver, I get he didn't care. You can kind of tell from the announcement, he didn't really make anything of it. He just announced me on the card as if I've always been a fighter there and people were kind of like, 'Wait, what?'

"So I feel like potentially, just based on how he behaves, I'm speculating here, that potentially he wasn't necessarily a fan of mine. And then on top of that, I didn't give him what he wanted as well. So yeah, there was no real relationship with Dana."

UFC didn't respond to ESPN's request for comment.

Page's UFC career wrapped up with a decision win over Nursulton Ruziboev amid boos from a partisan crowd in Paris last month.

Misfits wasn't the only promotion Page spoke to when looking at steps after the UFC with Jake Paul's Most Valuable Promotions among those interested in the Brit. Page said that a move to MVP, who has recently acquired MMA promotion PFL, was considered, but the timing wasn't right.

"Obviously that [MVP] was probably one of the things at the top of the list. But they just weren't in the right place right now," he said. "It wasn't the right timing more than anything. It wasn't just a financial thing, but it wasn't the right timing for them."

stories.headline: UCL Matchday 2: Viking FK and PSG impress; Man United a mess
stories.summary: The Chaaaaaampions! Europe's top competition returned with a ton of goals, a ton of big results and plenty to talk about. Let's start with the tiny Norwegian team that gave Bayern Munich a fright.
stories.body:
It is the way of the soccer world right now that competitions must get larger, with more teams, more matches per team and a much lower average reading on the jeopardy per match scale.

Aside from the obvious wear-and-tear concerns, I don't really mind this development. (Maybe it's the American in me: I'm used to bloat.)

I don't mind that the Euros have 24 teams, or that the Champions League has 36, or that the World Cup has 48 -- and that two-thirds of the competitors reach the knockout rounds in all of these tournaments. That has allowed for super-cool stories to develop.

Ukraine snuck into the knockout rounds at Euro 2020 (amid growing geopolitical stress) and then upset Sweden. Slovenia and Slovakia eked out advancement in 2024, too, and nearly pulled upsets. And while a huge Champions League with a huge set of knockout rounds has allowed more time for struggling powers like PSG and Manchester City in 2024-25 to rebound from poor starts, it also allowed Bodø/Glimt to find their footing and eventually take down Manchester City, Atlético Madrid and Inter Milan, consecutively, while nearly making the quarterfinals last season.

I don't mind bloat as long as it allows for proper storytelling and extra world-building. In a world with tilted finances, where only a few teams are actually capable of winning the whole thing, a fun journey almost matters more than the eventual destination.

Matchday 1 of this year's Champions League concerned me a bit in that regard. There was still fun to be had -- Como ran away from RB Leipzig in their first ever European group stage game, Real Madrid outlasted Inter Milan in a battle of European royalty, and 11 of 18 matches featured at least four goals. Goals are fun.

- UCL Talking Points: Who's to blame for Man United mess?

- Reaction: Man City can't compete with gold standard PSG

- Kirkland: Real Madrid did win, but glory feels far away

Still, Davids weren't exactly scoring damage points on Goliaths. PSG, Barcelona and Bayern Munich beat Slovan Bratislava, Feyenoord and Bodø/Glimt by a combined 16-2, and debutants LASK, Sabah and Viking all lost by a combined 8-1. It was a foreboding start, a sign that maybe Europe's giants have even further distanced themselves from the pack. I'm a fan of storytelling, and that's the least fun story to tell.

Luckily, Matchday 2 gave us delightful plot twists and track meets.

It also took us to Norway.

Main characters of the week

No. 1: Viking FK

Viking FK has lived a full club life since its founding in Stavanger in 1899: Early regional titles in the 1920s and 1930s; national titles in the 1950s, when that became a thing to aspire to; great spells (four straight titles in the 1970s); poor spells (relegation in 1986 and 2017); the requisite financial overextension in the 2010s (who among us).

On occasion, they've also enjoyed the glory of home European nights. They hosted Borussia Mönchengladbach (and drew 1-1) in the 1979-80 UEFA Cup, held Barcelona to a 0-0 draw in qualification for the inaugural 1992-93 Champions League) and walloped Sporting CP and drew with Werder Bremen in the 1999-2000 UEFA Cup. And in maybe the most famous night of the old Stavanger Stadion, they thumped Chelsea 4-2 in the 2002-03 UEFA Cup despite goals from Frank Lampard and John Terry.

Their current home, Viking Stadion, saw a win over Monaco in the 2005-06 UEFA Cup, plus a couple of fun victories in the 2022-23 Conference League. But after Tuesday, it's also the place where Viking hung three goals on -- and frustrated the hell out of -- Bayern Munich.

You have to take your victories where you can find them early in an eight-game Champions League league phase campaign, where the results aren't incredibly consequential and the surprises are minimal. But Viking vs. Bayern was an absolute blast. Viking ran the "score on your first shot" play -- every team should try that, it works out great for you -- and then went up 2-0 late in the first half. Bayern charged back because Bayern always charge back, but after a gorgeous Konrad Laimer-to-Luis Díaz goal gave the German giants the lead, Michael Olise got a red card, and it pretty visibly flipped the momentum in the match.

Herman Haugen headed in a tying goal over an unsuspecting Alphonso Davies (who probably should have been more suspecting), and Peter Christiansen forced a Jonas Urbig save in extra time. The stats for the game as a whole were one-sided (xG: Bayern 3.3, Viking 0.7), but when the match ended Viking appeared most likely to score next.

The Norwegian style of play might be the most aesthetically pleasing in the world at the moment: a mix of optimism and organization in attack, and a willingness to leave yourself a little exposed in the back. Bodø/Glimt have mastered this style and translated it well to European competitions -- they beat Borussia Dortmund on Wednesday to make it six straight home wins in the Champions League or Champions League qualification -- and Viking's first two Champions League league phase matches have featured 10 combined goals and a draw their fans will be talking about for ages.

I am a total sucker for stories like this.

And while we're celebrating teams that do everything possible to increase the pure entertainment value of the early stages, let's shout out Club Brugge, the watchability kings. So far they've lost 3-2 to Aston Villa and beaten Inter 4-3, and really, Tuesday's win undersold the amount of quality opportunities created: both teams underachieved against xG.

In 18 league phase matches since the start of 2024-25, they've scored multiple goals seven times and allowed multiple goals 10 times. They've won a match while allowing three, and they've drawn a match while scoring three. They are speed horses for this competition, and they are appreciated.

No. 2: Paris Saint-Germain

We're used to PSG taking their time shifting into gear in a given season. Luis Enrique has loads of both stars and incredible teenagers to give minutes to, and he knows he doesn't really have to find or lean on his best 11 until the spring. A few early losses won't exactly hurt them in Ligue 1, and two years ago they won the Champions League despite at one point going winless for four straight league phase matches.

They started this season in a little too much of a funk, however, with a loss to Lens in the Trophée des Champions and just two points in their first three Ligue 1 matches. They were tied for 13th with Le Mans after three league matchdays. That's a bit much.

Luckily, they know how to shift into gear.

In their last five matches on each side of the international break, they've won five matches by a combined 16-5. Enrique's still rotating like crazy -- 20 different guys have started in these five matches -- but PSG's ridiculous depth almost requires him to, and everyone's contributing. Ousmane Dembélé has three goals and four assists in four starts in this span, Ferran Torres has five goals, newcomer Maghnes Akliouche has two goals and an assist, Désiré Doué (who's still only 21, by the way) has a goal and two assists. Khvicha Kvaratskhelia hasn't contributed much, but PSG has still turned into a wrecking ball.

They seemed to have a point to prove on Wednesday in Manchester.

Visiting fellow petrol staters Manchester City, who are staring potentially epic penalties in the face, PSG went up 2-0 within 15 minutes thanks to goals from Doué and Dembélé and got a third from midfielder Vitinha before halftime. After Erling Haaland pulled one back for the home team, Akliouche put away an eventual 4-2 win with a goal in the 62nd minute.

City had won eight straight matches in all competitions and had humiliated Liverpool 3-0 at Anfield over the weekend, but PSG basically scored an early-round knockout. The xG figures favored City (2.6 to 1.8), but that can be pretty common when one team takes an early lead. At the time of Vitinha's goal, PSG had attempted eight of the match's 10 shots with a higher volume of touches in the attacking third. They were incredible, and they didn't need long to put the match away.

No. 3: Manchester United

In a way, Manchester United's 2-0 away loss to Atlético Madrid was like just about any other United match in 2026-27, in that the underlying stats that are usually pretty predictive weren't at all. Their xG differential was +0.8 in their 2-0 loss to Hull City to kick off the Premier League season, and in three matches with near-even xGDs, they've lost once with two draws. They're sixth in the Premier League in xG differential but 13th in the table, and at the time of Leny Yoro's 74th-minute red card in Madrid, they trailed 1-0 with a plus-0.4 xGD. (Atleti also ran the "Score on your first shot" play. I'm just saying, it's a great play!) The match turned one-sided after that.

Poor fortune and random, crippling mistakes are wrecking United's season when they really don't look too poor on paper.

Of course, United's players evidently have their own theory of what's going wrong, one revealed by Lisandro Martínez in postgame interviews. "We did a fantastic season last season and now we expect more from the top, more players to compete, because many teams bring many players as well," he said. "Atlético have an amazing team and they deserved to win today, but I expect more [investment] -- 100%. I expect more from our technical director."

Now, I know that other clubs have invested more than Manchester United in recent years, legally and illegally, and Martinez also made an interesting point about not "[staying] with what you did last season" because opponents always adjust. But despite the Premier League generally losing its mind from the perspective of cumulative transfer fees, I'm never going to see "completely rebuilding your midfield for €173.2 million," as United did this past summer, as a lack of investment or a simple "run it back" approach. United brought in Carlos Baleba, Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans in to address last year's biggest question mark; that's a pretty big change! And they've spent €1.1 billion in transfer fees alone over the past five years. A competent organization should be able to build a perfectly stable team with that.

Even if it's not really a lack of investment, though, United have definitely suffered from a lack of a plan, and it's made competent investment nearly impossible. There's been no ideological consistency in their managerial hires, and their common lineup this season includes two guys who signed or debuted for Louis van Gaal, one for Jose Mourinho, two for Ole Gunnar Solskjær, two for Erik ten Hag, three for Ruben Amorim and one for Michael Carrick. That's a diverse set of influences, and it can't be a surprise when a lack of a plan produces a lack of cohesiveness. But I guess none of what I'm saying is all that original, is it?

No. 4: Serie A

There are nine leagues with multiple Champions League entries this season. Three of them are averaging at least 2.0 points per game among their teams in the field: England's Premier League (2.4), Spain's LaLiga (2.4) and Germany's Bundesliga (2.0). After a perfect 5-for-5 in the wins department in Matchday 1 (followed by a 3-for-3 performance in the Europa League), the Premier League gave away some points this week thanks to the clubs in Manchester.

Four more leagues are averaging at least 1.0 points per game among their teams: France's Ligue 1 (1.5), Portugal's Primeira Liga (1.5), the Netherlands' Eredivisie (1.0) and Norway's Eliteserien (1.0). Hell yeah, Norway. Hanging out with the big boys.

Granted, some of those league successes are coming from one team -- PSG has six of Ligue 1's nine points, and Sporting CP has all six of the Primeira Liga's -- but it's still pretty damn noteworthy that we've gotten this far down the list without mentioning Serie A. After this week's 0-fer, with four losses from four matches, Italian teams now have four points from their first eight matches. Como thumped RB Leipzig in their Champions League home debut in September, and Roma managed a draw against a Fenerbahce team that got blown out by Aston Villa on Wednesday, and that's it.

Now, it's probably not as awful as it seems. Roma played well for 80 minutes against Real Madrid before getting Real Madrid'd at the end for a 4-3 defeat, and Como (lost 3-2 to Feyenoord), Inter (4-3 to Brugge) and Napoli (3-1 to Villarreal) all had at least slightly positive xG differentials, meaning that while their finishing lacked, they were creating equal or better chances than their opponents. But this is still a dire start for a league that has produced just one quarterfinalist in the last three tournaments. (Granted, Inter made the finals in 2025. But that's still it.)

Through two matches each, all four Italian teams have allowed at least two goals from high turnovers, and Roma are one of two teams (along with LASK) to have allowed three. Combined with the fact that the teams are a combined minus-2 in set piece goal differential, you could start to put together a case that Serie A teams aren't really keeping up with the tactical times. But I'll let that one marinate a bit longer before pursuing it further.

Best players of Matchday 2

One thing I like to do if I miss a given match is look at each player's combined xG + xPVA to see who did the most dangerous things in that match. I assume you know xG by now, but xPVA is basically everything else a player did to increase their team's chances of winning (or Expected Point Value), beyond shot attempts - passes, ball recoveries, tackles, et cetera. It's a useful at-a-glance tool, and I figured I'd share the top 15 most dangerous players of Matchday 2.

I enjoy that this is such a mix of expected and unexpected players. It's definitely not a surprise to see Liverpool's Bradley Barcola and Brugge's Nicolo Tresoldi making the list after their respective hat tricks, though Tresoldi evidently produced negative xPVA -- no progressive passes or carries or really anything else, just shots that went into the net. (And hey, if you're only going to do one thing, that's a good one.)

It probably also isn't a surprise that there are two other Brugge players on the list (Carlos Forbs and Romeo Vermant) considering how well they tore apart Inter's midfield. Lautaro had a brace against Brugge, but he could have had so much more: He attempted 12 shots worth 3.0 xG and put nine of those shots on goal. It was honestly one of the most prodigious performances you'll ever see.

There are plenty of familiar names elsewhere -- Erling Haaland, Atleti's Ademola Lookman, Arsenal's Eberechi Eze, Bayern's Luis Diaz -- but among the others let's shout out LASK's Florian Flecker (two goals in 45 minutes against Liverpool), Slavia's Lukás Provod (eight shots worth 1.4 xG, four on target, but somehow no goals) and Fenerbahce's Vedat Muriqi (two shots worth 0.9 xG).

And now, the Power Rankings

This is purely who I would pick if teams were playing this weekend.

1. Barcelona. Two wins and a 9-2 scoring margin thus far. In fact, in all competitions this season they have a perfect 10 wins from 10 matches, with a 43-9 scoring margin. Forty-three! Raphinha has 14 goals and three assists! Lamine Yamal has eight and nine! Fermín López has five and two! Karim Adeyemi has four and two! Anthony Gordon has two and four! Barca are pressing, passing and shooting better than ever, and while we'll have to wait and see if Hansi Flick's high-wire style can win a long series of knockout rounds, there is no question who the best team in Europe is at the moment.

We'll see if we're still saying that after next week: They visit PSG on Tuesday, then host Real Madrid for the first El Clásico of the season on Sunday.

2. PSG. Still only up to sixth in Ligue 1. I doubt they're worried.

3. Arsenal. Methodical and confident.

4. Bayern Munich. I'm not worried about them, but I'm not sure the "allow a goal in the first two minutes every match" approach of the last week is a good thing. (Missing Olise to a red card suspension for next week's Arsenal match stinks.)

5. Manchester City. Crush Liverpool and then get crushed by PSG. A pretty extreme week after a pretty extreme few weeks.

6. Real Madrid. If this isn't a damn "Real Madrid in the Champions League" chart, I don't know what is.

7. Aston Villa. After only one win in their first six matches in all competitions, they're now unbeaten in five, and they've scored 17 goals in the process.

8. Liverpool. It took Bradley Barcola until his seventh match to score in Liverpool red, but a hat trick made up for lost time.

9. Sporting CP. They haven't lost since April, and they've won each of their first two Champions League matches by multiple goals.

10. Atlético Madrid. Five straight wins since the loss to Liverpool.

11. VfB Stuttgart. They were handed a pretty light start -- Viking, at Slovan Bratislava -- and made the most of it with two easy wins. The challenges start with a visit from Atlético next week, but they're already two-thirds of the way toward advancing to the knockouts.

12. Real Betis. Two matches, two 3-2 wins. They drew 67,114 to the Estadio La Cartuja for the win over Porto on Wednesday, and it sounded like 100,000.

13. Borussia Dortmund. After six straight wins before the international break, they have a draw and a loss since. Someone always gets hit by the post-break funk.

14. Manchester United. I'm ranking them 14th because they're basically eighth and 20th at the same time.

15. Club Brugge. Averaging three goals for and three goals against. Hell yeah.

16. Como. They got xG'd against Feyenoord on Wednesday -- three goals allowed from 0.5 xG -- but they still play awfully pretty ball. They belong here.

17. Roma. They're still unbeaten in Serie A play, but their defense isn't holding up in this competition.

18. Villarreal. The Yellow Submarine can't get going in league play, but their finishing was on point against Napoli.

19. Inter Milan. Two one-goal losses isn't the end of the world, but I'd recommend beating Shakhtar next week.

20. RB Leipzig. The reverse Dortmund. RBL had lost three of four before the break and have won two by a combined 7-0 since their return.

21. Bodø/Glimt. Cue the "Chelsea Dagger!"

22. Porto. Their league form (eight matches, eight wins) means I'm not worried about their 0-for-2 start here. But upcoming home matches with PSV and Napoli are pretty big.

23. Lens. They've won only two of their last seven matches, and they have to visit Club Brugge next week.

24. Viking. My new lifelong favorite team.

25. PSV Eindhoven. Ivan Perisic played really well against RB Leipzig on Tuesday, but his failed penalty was a two-point miss in a one-goal loss.

26. Feyenoord. The crowd pop after a Feyenoord home goal is something else.

27. Galatasaray. The home crowd showed out against Barcelona as always, but the home team could only hold on for about 50 minutes.

28. Shakhtar Donetsk. Last year's Conference League semifinal run seems to have carried over. They have four points in two matches, and in their first "home" match at Chelsea's Stamford Bridge, they took the fight to AEK Athens awfully well.

29. Fenerbahçe. The 6-0 loss to Villa was exaggerated -- xG: Villa 3.1, Fenerbahce 1.9 -- but ... woof all the same.

30. Lille. Hey, they were tied with Arsenal for 60 minutes, at least.

31. Napoli. They're eighth in Serie A, and they're 33rd in xG differential after two matches here. Max Allegri was an unambitious hire, and the year sure hasn't started like he hoped.

32. AEK Athens. They had a chance to join the six-point club but could only hold onto a lead against Shakhtar for six minutes.

33. Sabah. They understood the assignment: Their home game with Slavia was probably the most winnable match on the docket, and a crowd of 29,670 showed up to Baki Olimpiya Stadionu to help make sure they won it.

34. LASK. Good: They kept fighting against Liverpool and grabbed a couple of late goals. Bad: They were down 6-1 at the time.

35. Slavia Prague. They're 0-for-2, and they still have to play No. 3, 4 and 7 on this list. Yikes.

36. Slovan Bratislava. They play at LASK on Nov. 3 and host Shakhtar on Dec. 9. If they want points in this competition, those are very important matches.

stories.headline: Rafael Câmara to Haas: How F1's next rookie could shake up Ferrari's future
stories.summary: The arrival of Rafa Camara to Haas will give Ferrari an interesting conundrum for the future, writes ESPN's Nate Saunders.
stories.body:
New Haas signing and Ferrari Driver Academy (FDA) star Rafael Câmara will continue his rapid career ascent as a Formula 1 rookie in 2027.

Câmara, 21, will replace Esteban Ocon at Haas next season and partner fellow FDA member Oliver Bearman.

The only way has been up for Câmara recently: he won the Formula 3 championship in 2025 and, as of the announcement of his signing, he leads the Formula 2 championship with two races to run.

The highly-rated Brazilian has been part of the FDA since 2022 -- that year he finished third in Italian F3 and was F1 championship leader Kimi Antonelli's teammate in the 2022 ADAC Championship, also finishing third.

Câmara comes from a racing family. His grandmother, Niége Rossiter, was a successful race driver in the Recife region and won races at a state level.

His elevation continues Brazil's proud F1 heritage -- he will become the nation's 34th driver, joining fellow compatriot Gabriel Bortoleto, who races for Audi.

Bortoleto's debut season had ended seven years without a Brazilian driver -- before Felipe Massa's retirement in 2017, there had been at least one on the grid every year stretching back to 1970.

A Ferrari audition season?

Haas' lineup will be a storyline worth keeping an eye on in 2027.

Putting Bearman and Câmara alongside each other in equal machinery will make a fascinating narrative in terms of who might one day end up racing for the Prancing Horse -- it will give Ferrari the clearest data comparison possible.

Haas has been a Ferrari customer since it made its Formula 1 debut in 2016 but has not had two drivers from the Italian team before.

Rising star Bearman made his debut for Haas in 2024 with two stand-in appearances for Kevin Magnussen before being signed to a full-time drive for 2025.

He has actually raced for Ferrari already, making his F1 debut as Carlos Sainz's stand-in earlier that season at the Saudi Arabian Grand Prix.

He has widely been seen as the next in line for Ferrari for some time, but an opening does not look likely to appear any time soon.

- 'Chucky' Verstappen is back. Luckily for Antonelli, it's too late

- F1 to return to Africa in 'early 2030s' as Rwanda race confirmed

- Ferrari protege Câmara completes Haas driver line-up for F1 2027

Charles Leclerc recently signed a bumper extension taking him into the 2030s, while seven-time world champion Lewis Hamilton has a contract until the end of 2027 at least -- sources have told ESPN there are options to continue beyond that and the growing feeling is that as things stand Hamilton will race for Ferrari beyond that time.

Bearman recently talked about how Hamilton's 2026 resurgence was good to see, but bad news in terms of his own prospects of moving up.

"As an F1 fan and a Lewis fan as well, it's pretty cool to see him performing at the level he is," Bearman told F1's Beyond the Grid podcast. "Seeing him on the top step in Barcelona was quite a special moment for British F1 in general. It was three Brits on the podium, with the best driver we've ever seen in P1. That's something pretty special.

"Of course, in terms of my future, that's not ideal. But I'm still young. I'm only 21. I'm not in a huge rush, and for me, staying at Haas for the foreseeable is not a bad thing. I feel like there's a lot to learn at this team. There's a lot to still achieve."

Bearman has comprehensively out-performed current teammate Ocon in their year and a half together and most will expect him to do the same against a rookie next year.

Should that not happen, Ferrari's next driver might not be such a safe bet.

stories.headline: Which NFL teams have never won a Super Bowl?
stories.summary: Some NFL teams have scored multiple Lombardi trophies, but which franchises have never won the Super Bowl? Check out more information now.
stories.body:
It's been 60 years since the NFL and AFL rival football leagues announced their merger and established the Super Bowl, the annual league championship that has been claimed by 20 different franchises since 1967.

Of the 12 organizations that are still looking to capture the elusive Vince Lombardi Trophy, four of them -- the Cleveland Browns, Detroit Lions, Houston Texans and Jacksonville Jaguars -- have never reached the big game.

The 2026 NFL season will culminate with Super Bowl LXI at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California, the home of the Los Angeles Rams and Los Angeles Chargers. The Rams, who won Super Bowl XXXIV in 2000 and Super Bowl LVI in 2022 (at SoFi Stadium), opened the campaign at +500 odds to win it all.

Let's take a closer look at the 12 franchises that have never won the big game (along with their number of Super Bowl appearances):

Cleveland Browns (0)

There was a time when the Browns were the class of the NFL, winning seven championships with three runner-up finishes in their first 10 years as a franchise. However, it's been a different story in the Super Bowl era, particularly over the last three decades. Cleveland reached the AFC Championship Game three times after the 1986, 1987 and 1989 seasons but lost all three to John Elway and the Denver Broncos -- often in heartbreaking fashion. Over the last 30 years, Cleveland has posted more winless seasons (one) than division titles and Super Bowl appearances combined (zero).

Detroit Lions (0)

The Lions are one of the NFL's oldest franchises (founded in 1930), yet they have zero Super Bowl appearances and arguably the worst postseason résumé in league history. That's why their 2023 run to the NFC Championship Game was such a big deal for Detroit fans. The Lions won their first playoff game since 1992, ending the NFL's longest active drought (and the fifth-longest all-time, right behind the team's previous 33-year winless run from 1958 to 1991). The Lions seemed poised to make their first Super Bowl appearance, but the San Francisco 49ers erased a 17-point deficit and defeated Detroit to punch their Super Bowl ticket.

Houston Texans (0)

The Texans are the newest franchise in the league, having joined as an expansion team in 2002, so Houston's inclusion on this list shouldn't come as much of a surprise. Still, it's been a tough couple of decades for the Texans, who have never reached a conference championship. However, that could change in the coming years, as rookie quarterback C.J. Stroud already looks like a potential superstar, while head coach DeMeco Ryans is a rising star himself and has Super Bowl experience from his time as an assistant coach in San Francisco. Their 45-14 wild-card win over Cleveland during the 2023-24 season helped Texans fans feel hopeful.

Jacksonville Jaguars (0)

The Jaguars have had a checkered history across nearly 30 years of existence. Shortly after they joined the NFL in 1995, they found immediate success, making the playoffs four times in their first five seasons -- including two trips to the AFC Championship Game. However, both ended in a lopsided defeat, and Jacksonville reached the playoffs just twice in the next 17 years before making another run to the AFC title game in the 2017 season -- only to blow a double-digit lead in the fourth quarter to Tom Brady's Patriots, squandering the team's best shot to reach a Super Bowl so far.

Arizona Cardinals (1)

Having been in existence since 1920, the Cardinals are the oldest franchise without a Super Bowl victory, though they did win two league championships (1925, 1947) prior to the Super Bowl era when they were based in Chicago. Arizona came oh-so close to its first Super Bowl victory in 2009, when star receiver Larry Fitzgerald scored a go-ahead touchdown with 2:37 left in Super Bowl XLIII. The Pittsburgh Steelers responded with one of the most impressive game-winning drives in Super Bowl history, scoring in the final seconds to sink the Cardinals' title hopes.

Los Angeles Chargers (1)

Few teams have done less with more than the Chargers, who have consistently boasted elite teams that come up short in the postseason. The franchise did reach the Super Bowl once in 1995, falling victim to Joe Montana's 49ers in a 49-26 rout. The Bolts also reached the AFC title game in the 1980 and 1981 seasons and again in 2007, losing by a touchdown or more in all three. While the Chargers have won 10 or more games six times in the last 20 years, they've won just five playoff games in that stretch, and their 12-19 playoff record ranks fourth-worst all-time. Will new coach Jim Harbaugh be able to end the drought?

Tennessee Titans (1)

While other franchises have seen a chance at a championship slip through their grasp, none have come closer than the Titans did in 2000. With six seconds left in Super Bowl XXXIV and Tennessee trailing by seven, receiver Kevin Dyson caught a slant pass over the middle and was wrapped up by St. Louis Rams linebacker Mike Jones near the 1-yard line. Dyson stretched out his arm toward the goal line, but he was inches short. The play, known as "The Tackle" or "One Yard Short," became the enduring image of that game and the Titans' years-long quest for their first Lombardi Trophy.

Atlanta Falcons (2)

While other teams on this list have reached more Super Bowls, none blew their chance at hoisting the Lombardi Trophy like the Falcons in 2017. Atlanta held a 28-3 lead over the New England Patriots in the third quarter of Super Bowl LI, when they boasted a win probability as high as 99.7%. That was before Tom Brady launched the defining comeback of his career, leading his team to the biggest comeback in Super Bowl history and the only overtime victory in the game's 57-year history. It was the second title game loss for the Falcons, who got blasted by the Denver Broncos in Super Bowl XXXIII. Still, nothing compares to that loss in '17, and the team has reached the playoffs just once in seven seasons since.

Carolina Panthers (2)

The Panthers have only been around since 1995, but they've reached the Super Bowl twice in their relatively brief existence. Both times, they were defeated by an all-time great quarterback. In 2004, Brady and the Patriots outlasted Carolina, 32-29, in Super Bowl XXXVIII. Twelve years later, Peyton Manning led the Broncos to a 24-10 win over the 15-1 Panthers in Super Bowl 50 -- his second Super Bowl victory and the final game of his storied career. Despite those gutting losses, Carolina remains the only team on this list with a winning record in the postseason and one of just 13 teams with multiple Super Bowl appearances this century.

Cincinnati Bengals (3)

The Bengals nearly worked their way off this list in 2022, when Joe Burrow led his team to Super Bowl LVI. However, the Bengals came up short against the Los Angeles Rams, 23-20. That marked Cincinnati's first Super Bowl appearance since 1989, when Montana led his 49ers to their second Super Bowl victory over the Bengals in an eight-year span -- with both games decided by five or fewer points. The Bengals were among the title favorites entering the 2023 season before Burrow suffered a season-ending right wrist injury.

Buffalo Bills (4)

No team has fallen short more often than the Bills, who lost four consecutive Super Bowls from 1991 to 1994 -- a run memorialized by the ESPN 30 for 30 documentary "Four Falls of Buffalo." The first was easily the most painful, as kicker Scott Norwood famously missed wide right on a 47-yard field goal in the final seconds to seal a 20-19 loss to the Giants in Super Bowl XXV. It would be the closest Buffalo came to a title, as they lost the next three Super Bowls by a combined 65 points (with none closer than 13 points). The cruelty of those losses is magnified by the fact that the Bills won the two final AFL championships (1964, 1965) before the introduction of the Super Bowl following the 1966 season.

Minnesota Vikings (4)

The Vikings are easily the most successful team on this list: Their 55% win percentage in the regular season ranks seventh all-time, and their four Super Bowl appearances are tied for the 13th-most in NFL history. Of course, their inclusion on this list makes all of those stats even more unsatisfying. Not only have they lost four Super Bowls, their six losses in conference championships are tied for fourth-most all time. All four of Minnesota's Super Bowl losses came in the 1970s. All six of their NFC title game losses have come since, including a 38-7 beatdown to the eventual champion Philadelphia Eagles in 2018.

stories.headline: After offseason chaos, the Red Wings have an 'us against the world' mentality
stories.summary: A captain's trade request, a key young player's holdout and a resigned general manager. Here's how the Red Wings are holding it all together.
stories.body:
All the Detroit Red Wings wanted was puck drop on a new season.

It was the only way.

The only way to -- finally -- turn the page on a tumultuous offseason of gossipy headlines that deposited Detroit under an unwelcome (and unrelenting) spotlight. There was captain Dylan Larkin's trade request in June, Steve Yzerman abruptly stepping down as general manager in July, key restricted free agent Simon Edvinsson remaining unsigned and no new front office leader in place until the announcement of interim general manager Shawn Horcoff just two days before training camp opened in late September.

The Red Wings -- fresh off missing the playoffs for a tenth straight year in 2025-26 -- limped their way into another preseason anyway. Larkin, stripped of the team's captaincy, was there but soon injured. Edvinsson, still without a contract, came to town as well (before going home to Sweden on the heels of his own trade request). It felt as though the drama was reaching a fever pitch faster than Detroit could get to that first real game, where the team's play -- and not some media machine -- could do the talking.

Promise. Hope. Belief. The Red Wings had it all just hours away from their first real outing. The slate would be clean, the energy refreshed.

"It's us against the rest of the world," defenseman Moritz Seider said. "That's something we've learned pretty fast; with how much noise there is around this team. I think there are plenty of reasons to be anxious or nervous. But it's like, even if we didn't know who the [full-time] GM was at the start of camp, like, what changes? Nothing, really, because he's not the one who's setting the standard, who's setting the tone on the ice, and he's definitely not going to go out there and help us to win games.

"We have everything in place to be a good hockey team, and it just comes down to each and every one of us to be the best version of ourselves. We have really come together as a group and feel we were just more excited than anything."

Seider and his teammates echoed similar allegiances of brotherhood and held tightly to them heading into player introductions before Game 1 of 84 was underway. But the assembled crowd at Little Caesars Arena didn't bring its rose-colored glasses (a plain-clothed Larkin receiving resounding boos during his pregame recognition? Foreshadowing!) because even before the team's coming display, the franchise's faithful was already despondent.

Because not getting a deal done with Edvinsson and having Larkin's situation unresolved weren't their only grievances with Detroit's front office. The Red Wings' season began with Alex DeBrincat as a key pending unrestricted free agent in July, and the club had whiffed on a mid-September deadline to get DeBrincat locked in on a maximum eight-year extension before the league's new collective bargaining agreement makes seven years the longest a player can agree on. Management also didn't retain fan favorite veterans such as Patrick Kane -- who walked back to Chicago in free agency -- and then to have Larkin lingering and now even available to play, it could suddenly feel like death by a thousand cuts for the franchise.

There was some good news coming. Detroit signed DeBrincat to a seven-year, $91 million deal Wednesday to help cushion the blow of its now 1-3-2 record -- but even that couldn't fully quell concerns over the Red Wings' tenuous prospects for the season.

Then Detroit actually began to play. And the knife poked in a little deeper. The Red Wings were bad -- so bad that midway through the 2-0 shutout loss to New York in their home opener, choruses of "sell the team" echoed (on multiple occasions) from inside a building (established in 2017) that still hasn't hosted an NHL postseason game. And Detroit hadn't even fallen to Rangers' star goaltender Igor Shesterkin. Backup Dylan Garand shut the door.

Game 2 of the year was another home loss (3-2 to Winnipeg). Detroit was 0-2 to start a season for the first time since 2015-16 (and then, at least, they'd been on the road). An injury to Marco Kasper (since placed on injured reserve with an upper-body injury) against the Jets loomed large. The Red Wings were fine at 5-on-5 but terrifically awful on special teams.

Basically, it was going to be a long year in Detroit. Or so it seemed. But the Red Wings had miles to go before being truly counted out. Larkin would be back for their third game of the season. The kinship -- which had been a rallying cry for players repeatedly in the past -- was still intact. All Detroit needed was to ignore the mounting sense of crisis, clean up its early incompetence, win a few games and get on track toward what was supposed to be the year when it turned everything around against all odds.

It was now or never all too soon for Detroit to put actions behind words. That remains -- like the Red Wings -- a work in progress. There will be no reprieve then for a group that has been taking it on the chin from detractors for months. The Red Wings have to show that true change is not only still possible but also probable.

That has meant being realistic about what they are and aren't while uncovering an evolving identity. Whatever Detroit intends to become must be forged from less-than-ideal circumstances. The time, as ever, was nigh.

"I think we've done a pretty good job keeping the noise out of here," DeBrincat said. "I think we know what we can do. Maybe we deserve better in these games, a couple more bounces can go our way. But we have to work for it. It's not just going to come to us. We're not skilled enough to expect to go out there and score six goals. We have to be more crisp and bring that mentality a little bit higher. We'll be good. We're in the right spots, we're just not executing on the plays and we're not putting it in the net. We have plenty of chances to win these games."

From his lips, to the hockey gods' ears.

DETROIT NEEDED A VICTORY. In more ways than one.

During NHL draft weekend in June, it was a shocking development when news leaked that Larkin had asked for a trade from the club that drafted him 15th overall in 2014. The team's top center, who has amassed 645 points in 811 career games with 30-plus goals in each of his last five seasons, has five years remaining on his eight-year, $69.6 million contract that includes a no-trade clause.

Larkin originally said he wanted to land only in Vegas, Florida or Minnesota. However, he reportedly widened the net to include Dallas, Washington, Colorado and Tampa Bay, leaving Yzerman (and now Horcoff) with scant leverage to gain an adequate return on the team's star player. And so, Larkin remains a Red Wing -- albeit one without a letter -- and, as such, one of their best forwards. Having Larkin healthy after he suffered an upper-body injury working out in the gym was best for Detroit's prospects on the ice.

Larkin was cleared to return for Detroit before the Red Wings faced Ottawa. He didn't miss a beat, scoring a goal in the first period and adding an assist on Viktor Arvidsson's power-play strike in the second period to help Detroit earn its 5-3 win that delivered a much-needed shot in the arm after its frustrating start.

It meant something to have Larkin involved in a positive turn of events for the team. Granted, the cloud hanging over his unfulfilled ask isn't going to miraculously dissipate. But until it comes to fruition (or not), the Red Wings don't want to fracture internally. Larkin acknowledged during the preseason that, "I asked for a trade from the Detroit Red Wings as a captain and that has consequences" and expressed that, through his actions, he wanted to "build trust with my teammates again and with the fans."

That is why he went out with the others during those poorly received player introductions before the season opener. Larkin had to expect his presence would spark some displeasure. But he went out there anyway. Coach Todd McLellan could sympathize with the heat Larkin took, knowing too it wasn't entirely undeserved or unexpected.

"Dylan, today, being a part of the team, he wanted to be out there for the ceremony," McLellan said after Detroit's first loss. "Dylan's explanation was, 'I don't want the rest of my teammates, the ones that aren't dressed, to not be out there,' so, we went out as a team. Obviously, he's got to live with the ramifications of asking for a trade. It's not comfortable for anybody. I feel bad for him, I do."

Winning, though, is a salve. It has the power to reduce some friction. There is no doubt Detroit's lineup is strongest with Larkin in it, and his interactions with teammates (who have carefully toed the line with their own comments on his whole mess) remain characteristically jocular.

It was a pleasant realization for McLellan that by the end of training camp, the Red Wings' room wasn't badly splintered after what had been said -- and not done -- all summer. Those individual bonds forged through the years seemingly remained -- and were perhaps tight enough to also see Detroit past some early-season adversity.

"With everything that's going on around our organization -- and there's been a lot -- just the unity of the players right now is fairly good," McLellan said ahead of the Red Wings' final preseason game. "I had some concern about that. Not that they were going to be torn apart, but just how they were going to deal with all of this stuff, and to this point, in the locker room, the practices, the intermingling that I do with the group, they're handling it fairly well, and I don't want to say that's a surprise, but that's good to see and hear. But we'll still have some rough water ahead of us, and we're going to have to deal with things."

McLellan spoke with the weariness of a coach who has been there -- in the darkest depths of a freefall -- with his team. Maybe he is still a little haunted. Maybe he will be again.

Detroit's bench boss saw his team squander its promise just last season, starting the campaign quite opposite this one. The Red Wings stormed off then with nine wins in their first 13 games and were primed to snap out of their playoff doldrums. When the league halted on Feb. 6 for its Olympic break, the Red Wings sat third in the Atlantic and seventh in the NHL with 72 points. But Detroit returned to the ice three weeks later and dropped straight off a cliff, cratering defensively and sputtering offensively, so that the woeful 8-12-4 record it produced through the final 24 games (good for 28th overall in that stretch) left it once again on the outside looking in.

It was another lost season. Another missed opportunity. And the failure naturally played a part in Larkin -- now 30 years old and with only five postseason appearances to his credit from a long-ago rookie campaign -- antsy to move out of the Motor City. If Larkin was possibly feeling revitalized along with his teammates to secure that first victory of the season and put up a united front of sorts against the proverbial onslaught, the sentiment wouldn't last long.

Detroit dropped its next game (a fourth straight home outing) to Seattle 6-3. Then the Red Wings finally got on the road to Montreal in their first back-to-back of the year, but found their luck unchanged in a 1-0 shootout loss.
