stories.headline: AFL trade and free agency grades - Every club's report card from the 2026 transfer period
stories.summary: The 2026 AFL trade and free agency period is over. Some teams improved, some stagnated, and others, well, got worse. Here's how every team fared over the last two weeks.
stories.body:
The 2026 AFL trade and free agency period is complete. Some teams improved, some have stagnated, and others, well, seemed to have gotten worse.

READ: Every player move from the 2026 off-season

Here's how every team fared over the last two weeks:

Adelaide
Incoming: N/A

Outgoing: Jordon Butts, Luke Pedlar

2026 draft selections: 15, 32, 35, 43, 56, 92

I'm not sure what the Crows' gameplan was this trade and free agency period, but it's fair to say the club sat on its hands and did next to nothing. Losing key defender Jordon Butts to the Bulldogs obviously weakens them, while just one draft selection inside the top 30 is unlikely to provide much immediate support. Adelaide's list profile remains fine, and maybe they will surprise us all in 2027, but you just get the sense so many other clubs have passed them by over the last two weeks.

Grade: F

Brisbane
Incoming: N/A

Outgoing: Lachie Neale, Sam Marshall, Will McLachlan, Keidean Coleman

2026 draft selections: 21, 27, 28, 45, 79, 97

The Lions were the biggest winners of last year's off-season (and season!), but this year was a different story. All year it seemed a formality they would lose the services of dual Brownlow Medal winner Lachie Neale, who ultimately signed with Collingwood as a free agent. They also waved goodbye to Keidean Coleman and Sam Marshall, two players who had struggled to crack the best 23 of late. No picks inside the top 20 would be concerning for 17 other clubs, but the Lions still have so much young talent at their disposal and are primed to challenge again in 2027.

Grade: C-

Carlton
Incoming: Joel Amartey, Lachie Whitfield

Outgoing: Hudson O'Keeffe, Flynn Riley

2026 draft selections: 13, 18, 31, 50, 61, 72, 90

The Blues addressed two areas of weakness this off-season. The addition of free agent Joel Amartey provides spearhead Harry McKay with a stable forward line partner, while the Lachie Whitfield signing offers run, experience, and a kick-first option off halfback, the perfect piece to fit into Josh Fraser's system. Carlton really didn't give up much to land Whitfield, either. And barring Essendon taking a stab at talented father-son prospect Cody Walker with pick No. 1, the club has also ensured it has enough draft capital to match any bids that will come for him.

Grade: A

Collingwood
Incoming: Lachie Neale, Jesse Hogan, Flynn Riley

Outgoing: Scott Pendlebury

2026 draft selections: 11, 30, 67, 68, 70, 88

The Magpies had been crying out for a true inside midfielder, and they landed arguably the best in the competition in Lachie Neale. The two-time Brownlow Medal winner is an elite ball winner and clearance player, and should perfectly complement superstar Nick Daicos. Collingwood also signed Jesse Hogan, a man that won the Coleman Medal just two years ago, and gave up virtually nothing for him. The loss of champion Scott Pendlebury obviously stings, but you have to feel this club is in a stronger position now than it was two weeks ago.

Grade: A

Essendon
Incoming: Jack Bowes, Keidean Coleman

Outgoing: Zach Merrett, Jordan Ridley

2026 draft selections: 1, 17, 25, 80

Former skipper Zach Merrett finally got his wish of a fresh start at the Hawks, while fellow experienced player Jordan Ridley also departs the club for the Cats. The additions of Jack Bowes and Keidean Coleman are fine, but are either going to be difference makers in a side that's been languishing at the bottom of the ladder for several years? I'm not so sure. The only saving grace for the Bombers is that they hold pick No. 1. They simply have to make the most of that selection.

Grade: D

Fremantle
Incoming: Dom Bedendo

Outgoing: Nathan O'Driscoll

2026 draft selections: 19, 40, 60, 63, 78, 96

The Dockers were incredibly quiet during the trade and free agency window, but that's not exactly a bad thing. Remember, if not for Will Ashcroft and Logan Morris, Fremantle win the 2026 premiership. There was absolutely no reason for the Dockers to panic and overpay for someone after their Grand Final heartbreak, instead, this club, with its plethora of youth and talent, should feel as if it can contend for years to come. Trust the process and go again in 2027.

Grade: C

Geelong
Incoming: Toby Greene, Jordan Ridley, Rowan Marshall

Outgoing: Jack Bowes

2026 draft selections: 36, 57, 62, 75, 93

Every year the Cats just find a way to bring big names through the door, and 2026 was no exception. Rowan Marshall was tipped to join 12 months ago and finally makes the move from St Kilda to bolster the club's ruck stocks. Toby Greene adds class, experience, and unrivalled goal-kicking nous to the forward line. Jordan Ridley is a stable and still wildly underrated defensive asset. The best part? To land this trio the club only had to give up midfield depth piece Jack Bowes, and some draft capital. They won't be much of a feature at the upcoming draft, but they don't have to be. These Cats are in win-now mode.

Grade: A

Gold Coast Suns
Incoming: Scott Pendlebury, Aidan Schubert, Sam Butler

Outgoing: Ben King

2026 draft selections: 8, 85

Scott Pendlebury might be a champion of the game, but there's no denying the Suns just got worse. The addition of 38-year-old Pendlebury doesn't outweigh the seismic loss of spearhead Ben King, a man who has booted 230 goals over the last four seasons. How do they replace him? Perhaps it's the incoming Aidan Schubert, but he's years away from having a real impact. Making matters worse, it seems Brownlow medallist Matt Rowell is likely to request a trade back to Victoria at the end of next season. This club is in a real precarious spot right now. A penny for Christian Petracca's thoughts...

Grade: C-

GWS Giants
Incoming: N/A

Outgoing: Toby Greene, Kieren Briggs, Jesse Hogan, Lachie Whitfield

2026 draft selections: 9, 20, 26, 59, 77, 86

Just two years ago Toby Greene, Kieren Briggs, Jesse Hogan, and Lachie Whitfield were probably four of the Giants' most important players. None of them remain at the club after an action-packed trade and free agency window, with GWS instead opting to clear out and trust the youth underneath. It's a move that will either make the Giants look like geniuses or total fools, but even those who are incredibly bullish about the approach would concede there is likely to be some pain on the immediate horizon.

Grade: D

Hawthorn
Incoming: Zach Merrett, Ben King, Josh Goater

Outgoing: Finn Maginness, Aidan Schubert, Sam Butler, Bodie Ryan

2026 draft selections: 29, 37, 71, 94

The Hawks should probably be the 2027 flag favourites after a whirlwind two weeks that's seen them finally land former Essendon skipper Zach Merrett, as well as Ben King. Merrett adds depth, experience, and A-grade ball use to Hawthorn's midfield group, while King provides a focal point in attack, taking the burden off the ageing Jack Gunston. Sure, Hawthorn gave up some depth, but their best 23 has improved out of sight and they still have draft collateral over the next few years to ensure talent keeps coming through the door.

Grade: A+

Melbourne
Incoming: Zane Duursma, Will McLachlan, Bodie Ryan

Outgoing: Jack Viney, Trent Rivers

2026 draft selections: 4, 14, 48, 52

Just about everyone panicked when the Demons farewelled premiership heroes Christian Petracca and Clayton Oliver last year, and look how that turned out. This club seems to have a plan for the future and it isn't prepared to compromise on what it wants. Melbourne has nailed its draft picks in recent times and with selections four and 14 this year, you'd expect two more highly talented prospects to join the ranks. Who knows if Zane Duursma will work out, but they've landed him for a fraction of what the Kangaroos gave up at the draft three years ago. It's a low risk punt worth taking.

Grade: C

North Melbourne
Incoming: Nick Blakey

Outgoing: Zane Duursma, Josh Goater

2026 draft selections: 33, 49, 66, 74, 84

Credit to the Kangaroos, they finally landed a big name. The only problem is I'm not sure Nick Blakey is the superstar many are claiming. There's no doubt Blakey will add drive and dash off halfback, but is he the player you look to in the closing stages of a tight game? North also gave up a truckload of future draft capital to get him through the door which will hurt them in the coming years. And then there's the Zane Duursma fiasco. Losing a player the club invested pick No. 4 in just three years ago is an unmitigated disaster. With no selections inside the top 30 this year, it will be a rare draft without the Roos being a major player.

Grade: C+

Port Adelaide
Incoming: Luke Pedlar

Outgoing: Zak Butters

2026 draft selections: 7, 12, 22, 24, 34, 46, 65

You're never going to feel great when a player of Zak Butters' class and calibre walks out the door, but the silver lining for Port Adelaide is that Dougie Cochrane should be set to walk back in. The academy talent is the consensus best player in the upcoming draft and the Power are in a position to match any bids on their man. Expect Port to be heavily involved in the draft over the next couple of years as they look to rebuild around the likes of Cochrane, Connor Rozee, and Jason Horne-Francis.

Grade: B

Richmond
Incoming: Kieren Briggs, Nathan O'Driscoll

Outgoing: N/A

2026 draft selections: 2, 5, 44, 81

The Tigers found Toby Nankervis' successor in Kieren Briggs, who crosses from the Giants as a free agent. That's a nice win. Nathan O'Driscoll was unable to find a place in Fremantle's best team of late but should receive far more opportunity in the black and yellow jumper in 2027. Richmond has two more picks inside the top five, though they are likely to be shuffled down a few spots with bid matching on Dougie Cochrane and Cody Walker, and they simply must nail them. Even still, this side will remain incredibly young in 2027.

Grade: C

St Kilda
Incoming: Sam Marshall

Outgoing: Rowan Marshall

2026 draft selections: 10, 16, 41, 51, 69, 87

The Saints went all-in last year, signing Tom De Koning, Jack Silvagni, Liam Ryan, and Sam Flanders. They weren't nearly as busy this off-season, and few expected them to be. Long-time ruck Rowan Marshall departs the club for the Cats, while Sam Marshall joins and should bolster their midfield stocks. Outside of that, St Kilda will be hoping to cash in with their two first round draft selections. If not, it could spell the end of Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera's tenure. This team wouldn't want to be starting 2027 slowly...

Grade: C

Sydney Swans
Incoming: N/A

Outgoing: Joel Amartey, Nick Blakey

2026 draft selections: 6, 38, 39, 47, 54, 76, 95

Two best 23 players departed the Swans this past fortnight with halfback Nick Blakey being traded to the Kangaroos and key forward Joel Amartey signing with the Blues as a free agent. Don't forget, Callum Mills is unlikely to suit up for the entire year after suffering an ACL injury during this year's finals campaign. That's three best 23 players to replace! Who knows what's happening with Isaac Heeney and Chad Warner? Swans fans will be praying for a hit with pick No. 6 at the upcoming draft to soften the blow.

Grade: C-

West Coast Eagles
Incoming: Jack Viney, Trent Rivers

Outgoing: N/A

2026 draft selections: 3, 23, 58, 64, 73, 82

It's clear the Eagles don't want to take the same approach as the Tigers and rely solely on the kids. Instead, they're continuing to add experienced pieces around their young talent in an effort to ease the rebuild and avoid a nosedive in morale. Jack Viney and Trent Rivers add premiership experience to the club and they haven't had to give up too much to get them. West Coast will feature prominently at November's draft with pick No. 3, 23, as well as a compensation pick in the likely scenario that the club's first selection is pushed back by a bid.

Grade: C+

Western Bulldogs
Incoming: Jordon Butts, Finn Maginness, Hudson O'Keeffe, Zak Butters

Outgoing: N/A

2026 draft selections: 42, 53, 55, 83, 89, 91

The Bulldogs now possess the most dynamic midfield trio in the game with Zak Butters joining skipper Marcus Bontempelli and Ed Richards in the red, white, and blue. It's a marquee signing for Luke Beveridge's team that simply has to put them into premiership contention. Jordon Butts also joins the club and will bolster what's traditionally been a weaker defensive unit. Don't forget about key forward star Sam Darcy, who will return from a season-ending ACL injury.

Grade: A+

stories.headline: 'All love': All Blacks inspiring NZ's Rugby League World Cup tilt
stories.summary: Buoyed by a visit from their All Blacks brothers, Stacey Jones's ambitious Kiwis are out to open the rugby league World Cup with a bang by completing a memorable New Zealand double over Australia.
stories.body:
Buoyed by a visit from their All Blacks brothers, Stacey Jones's ambitious Kiwis are out to open the rugby league World Cup with a bang by completing a memorable New Zealand double over Australia.

Five days after the All Blacks crushed the Wallabies 50-19 to clinch the Bledisloe Cup for a 23rd straight year, the Kiwis and Kangaroos clash in a trans-Tasman blockbuster in Sydney on Thursday night to kick off the global showpiece.

Eight ABs, including superstar winger Will Jordan and playmaker Cam Roigard, cast aside the cross-code rivalry to drop into New Zealand's captain's run on Wednesday and throw their support behind Jones's side.

"It's just all love and supporting each other and hopefully we can go watch their game on Saturday too, so it's pretty special," New Zealand captain James Fisher-Harris said.

"How dominant and how they go about their business and represent New Zealand, there's a lot of things that they do that we look up to so yeah, it's pretty cool."

Leading what he believes is "potentially" the best Kiwi forward pack ever, Fisher-Harris says "the plan" is to lift the World Cup and, like the Warriors, continue to inspire a whole new generation of rugby league players back in their homeland just like the 2008 winners did.

"When they won in 2008, I was watching Blairy (Adam Blair) and that, (Nathan) Cayless and obviously Benji (Marshall), so that made me want to go down this path," the enforcer said.

"So hopefully we can do something like that. When you are successful like that, it gets you motivated and you want to play for a certain team or a certain code.

"So that's the plan anyways, to be successful in this World Cup."

Behind the monster pack will be Kayln Ponga for the first time after the talismanic fullback, at 28, opted to represent his parents' homeland.

"He's playing pretty good right about now," Fisher-Harris said of Ponga, who led Newcastle on their magical run from seventh to a 19-18 grand final loss to the Sydney Roosters.

"But it's not just his playing ability, it's his leadership and he's been in the game for a while now.

"He's won a few things but it looks like he's pretty keen to get in that black and white jersey."

Coach Stacey Jones also believes Australia's loss is very much New Zealand's gain.

"For the Knights this year and particularly the back end of the season, he carried them to a grand final," Jones said.

"Obviously had a lot of support around him, but he's got a lot of confidence in his game at the moment and we're just lucky that we've got him on our side."

stories.headline: What NBA preseason has revealed about the Lakers, 76ers, Celtics and every team
stories.summary: With 2026-27 tipoff closing in, Ben Golliver shares the key takeaways that will shape the regular season.
stories.body:
The NBA preseason is a time to welcome new faces, sort through lineup questions, hype up prospects, squabble over unresolved contract situations and panic about unfortunate injuries before the real competition begins.

With Tuesday's openers fast approaching, let's bounce around the league one final time in search of key takeaways that will shape the upcoming season.

Jump to a team:

ATL | BOS | BKN | CHA | CHI | CLE

DAL | DEN | DET | GS | HOU | IND

LAC | LAL | MEM | MIA | MIL | MIN

NO | NYK | OKC | ORL | PHI | PHX

POR | SAC | SA | TOR | UTAH | WAS

Atlanta Hawks
The preseason revealed ... the backcourt is loaded

With Trae Young's salary no longer on the books, the Hawks have assembled a backcourt rotation stacked with creators Nickeil Alexander-Walker and CJ McCollum, stoppers Dyson Daniels and Lu Dort, shooter Corey Kispert and 2026 lottery pick Kingston Flemings. In fact, Atlanta had such a surplus that it traded two backup guards to land 3-and-D forward Dorian Finney-Smith from the Charlotte Hornets in September.

Hawks coach Quin Snyder has used multiple starting lineups during the preseason, but he's best served sticking with last season's top group -- Alexander-Walker, McCollum, Daniels, Jalen Johnson and Onyeka Okongwu -- because it posted a phenomenal plus-20.3 net rating. That would move Dort to a reserve role after he spent the past six seasons as a starter for the Oklahoma City Thunder.

Boston Celtics
The preseason revealed ... Jayson Tatum will hit the ground running

While Tatum returned from a May 2025 Achilles tear in less than 10 months, his shot looked rusty and he played below his All-NBA standard down the stretch last season. Then, his speedy comeback ended with a whimper when he sat out a Game 7 loss to the Philadelphia 76ers in the first round due to left knee discomfort.

By taking those lumps last season, Tatum prepared himself for a smoother launch in 2026-27. The five-time All-Star was spectacular at times while posting 23 points in 27 minutes during his preseason debut, and his outside shot looked confident in a variety of situations. The Celtics must learn to live without Jaylen Brown and incorporate two key new pieces in forward Paul George and center Mitchell Robinson, but everything will be easier if Tatum is back to performing like an MVP contender.

Brooklyn Nets
The preseason revealed ... Egor Demin is one to watch

Be sure to include Demin on the list of 2025 first-round picks poised for major improvement in their second campaigns. While draft classmates in Dallas' Cooper Flagg and San Antonio's Dylan Harper are bursting with star potential, Demin's goal will be to move past a shaky rookie season and establish himself as a quality starting point guard.

After being content to settle for outside shots as a rookie, the 20-year-old Russian was more forceful off the dribble at Las Vegas summer league. That shift was evident in a preseason win over the 76ers: Midway through the first quarter, Demin drove past LeBron James and finished a difficult layup over Joel Embiid. Veteran forwards Michael Porter Jr. and Julius Randle will handle the bulk of the scoring for Brooklyn, but Demin is arguably the Nets' most important player given his ability to shape their rebuilding effort.

Charlotte Hornets

The preseason revealed ... life without Kon Knueppel is no fun

While Knueppel's record 3-point shooting got all the attention during his rookie season, his reliability was just as important to Charlotte's success. Knueppel averaged 18.5 points per game in 81 appearances, joining Young and Karl-Anthony Towns as the only rookies to hit those scoring and availability marks over the past decade. And despite Knueppel's youth and starter responsibilities, the 2025 No. 4 pick posted a strong plus-6.2 net rating.

Unfortunately, Knueppel has been sidelined throughout the preseason with a hamstring injury and his availability for opening night remains uncertain. Knueppel is a critical player for the retooling Hornets, who pivoted by trading star guard LaMelo Ball to the Minnesota Timberwolves this summer. Charlotte's offense won't sing at full volume until its most prolific shooter is back to 100%.

Chicago Bulls

The preseason revealed ... Caleb Wilson will stop you in your tracks

There's a special joy in watching Wilson explore the bounds of his developing game. Already in his first preseason, the 2026 No. 4 pick has raced out in transition for thunderous dunks, worked through traffic for turnaround midrange jumpers and created space in isolation to launch step-back 3-pointers. That range of offensive skills is rare for a 6-foot-10 rookie forward.

Wilson has a path to becoming the best player in a strong class if he solidifies his outside shooting and smooths out his ballhandling and decision-making. His confidence out of the gate is a positive indicator, and he appears destined to be an impact defender given his length and leaping ability. The Bulls face no immediate pressure to win after changing their general manager and coach, so this season will be all about gawking at Wilson's latest highlights and daydreaming about his potential.

Cleveland Cavaliers
The preseason revealed ... Peyton Watson isn't the only notable newcomer

Get this: The Cavaliers will pay their projected starters more than $179 million in 2026-27, well above this year's $165 million salary cap. Given that top-heavy spending structure, Cleveland will welcome any and all second-unit help.

While Watson was the Cavaliers' biggest offseason addition and plugs in as a starting forward, Mario Hezonja also arrived this summer as a bargain signing after spending the past six seasons in Europe. The 31-year-old Hezonja, who once upon a time was a 2015 lottery pick, averaged 17.5 points per game for Real Madrid in Spain's ACB league last season. His primary task will be to boost Cleveland's bench scoring, which ranked 25th in 2025-26, with his inside-outside versatility.

Dallas Mavericks

The preseason revealed ... the Cooper Flagg hype train is gaining speed

ESPN's Brian Windhorst ably documented Flagg's eye-opening performances during the Mavericks and Rockets' exhibitions at the NBA China Games. While it would be foolish to read too much into preseason statistics, Flagg averaged 25.8 points, 7.8 rebounds, 7.8 assists plus more than a steal and a block per 36 minutes in the two games. Only one player in NBA history has maintained those per-game averages for a full regular season: LeBron James.

The No. 1 pick in the 2025 draft should factor heavily into this year's All-Star conversation, and there's a good chance Flagg will outperform his No. 23 spot in ESPN's NBA Rank if he continues to impact games on both ends like he did in Macao. Flagg's 3-point shot -- he hit under 30% as a rookie -- can still improve, but his combination of instincts, athleticism and work ethic is rare. And remember: He's still a teenager.

Denver Nuggets

The preseason revealed ... Nikola Jokic's passing is getting more preposterous

Jokic delivered the best highlight of the preseason when he casually flipped a no-look, behind-the-back pass from the left baseline past three Utah Jazz defenders to find Cameron Johnson for a right-corner 3. The assist was so on the money that Johnson seemingly didn't move his hands an inch to haul it in, and the crowd was already roaring before the shot went up.

The play was a good reminder that the three-time MVP is entering rarified air as a passer. Jokic led the NBA in assists per game for the first time last season, and the 31-year-old ranks first among centers in career assists. Though Jokic enters the season ranking 41st on the NBA's all-time assist leaderboard, he's only about five seasons away from reaching the top 10 at his recent pace. Somehow, a Serbian center who wasn't selected until the second round of the 2014 draft has a legitimate chance of surpassing all-time great point guards such as Oscar Robertson and Magic Johnson.

Detroit Pistons
The preseason revealed ... cooler heads prevailed in the Jalen Duren saga

While the negotiations weren't pretty and dragged past media day, Detroit avoided all the nightmare scenarios by finally inking the All-Star center to a five-year, $200 million contract extension on Oct. 1. The Pistons didn't fork over anything close to max money, they don't need to worry about Duren playing half-heartedly on a qualifying offer, and he can't walk next summer as an unrestricted free agent. Detroit's core of Cade Cunningham, Duren and Ausar Thompson is officially locked in for years to come.

Duren took a major step to move past the ordeal by stating that he's a "Detroit Piston for life" during a conciliatory news conference. Now, the focus shifts back to the court, where expectations will be sky-high following the Pistons' 60-win campaign in 2025-26. Duren's role shouldn't change dramatically, though his defensive impact could come under greater scrutiny after Detroit traded backup center Isaiah Stewart to the Memphis Grizzlies in June.

Golden State Warriors

The preseason revealed ... Podz got paid

The Warriors' pile of questions got only bigger during the preseason due to Kristaps Porzingis' mysterious indefinite absence just months after Golden State signed him to a two-year, $40 million contract. Warriors coach Steve Kerr is already trying to get by without injured star Jimmy Butler III, and Porzingis' availability concerns feel like a blow this roster can't sustain.

In brighter news, 23-year-old guard Brandin Podziemski signed a five-year, $110 million rookie extension earlier this month. While the confident scorer is less accomplished than most of the other players from the 2023 draft who inked extensions this cycle, his signing reflects Golden State's need to prepare for the future with Stephen Curry, Butler, Draymond Green and Al Horford all approaching the twilight of their careers. Podziemski's $22 million AAV puts him in the same ballpark as fellow guards Christian Braun, Malik Monk and CJ McCollum. Within that group last season, Podziemski ranked first in win shares and second in scoring.

Houston Rockets

The preseason revealed ... Fred VanVleet is back with a bang

The Rockets took a lot of heat when their offense fell flat in last season's playoffs due to spacing and playmaking concerns. In his preseason debut, VanVleet wasted no time reminding observers that he remains Houston's best solution. After missing last season with a knee injury, VanVleet posted 17 points and seven assists to key a convincing exhibition win over the Mavericks in his first game action in nearly 18 months.

The 32-year-old point guard launched 12 3-pointers, twice as many as Houston's other starters combined. VanVleet's return should produce some trickle-down benefits: Kevin Durant and Alperen Sengun will have another trustworthy ball handler for late-clock and late-game situations, and Reed Sheppard should enjoy cleaner looks when he plays alongside the veteran floor general.

Indiana Pacers

The preseason revealed ... Tyrese Haliburton can still tug on the heartstrings

Haliburton's Achilles tear during Game 7 of the 2025 Finals was one of the most heartbreaking and consequential in-game injuries in NBA history. The underdog Pacers were knocking on the doorstep of their first championship after a series of miracle playoff comebacks, only for their All-Star guard to go down with an injury that also cost him the entire 2025-26 season.

Fast-forward to last week: Haliburton made his preseason debut against the Minnesota Timberwolves at Iowa State, his alma mater. The former Cyclones star purchased thousands of tickets to fill the student sections and thanked the crowd before scoring seven points and dishing six assists in limited minutes. "It's been 472 days since I've played a game of basketball," he said. "I wouldn't want to do it anywhere else except my second home." The heartwarming scene in Ames was the perfect way for Haliburton to complete his grueling injury rehabilitation and get back to work.

LA Clippers

The preseason revealed ... Darius Garland had better have a career year

The Clippers' injury news went from bad to worse when guard Max Strus suffered a right foot injury just five minutes into the first quarter of their preseason opener. Strus, who is expected to miss at least a month, joins teammates Brandon Ingram, Jordan Miller and Yanic Konan Niederhauser with long-term injuries. Meanwhile, Bradley Beal has been sidelined this preseason with right knee inflammation.

To make matters worse, five of the Clippers' top six scorers from last season are no longer on the team, leaving Garland, a two-time All-Star point guard, as the last man standing. A passable offense will hinge on Garland shifting to a score-first mindset to compensate for the lack of firepower around him. While Rui Hachimura and rookie Keaton Wagler should also enjoy green lights, LA's offense will likely be a grind until Ingram returns.

Los Angeles Lakers
The preseason revealed ... surprisingly, title talk is in the air

The Lakers are brimming with optimism after a transformative offseason, during which LeBron James departed and a new cast of role players arrived in Hollywood. Luka Doncic and coach JJ Redick have both floated championship aspirations, even though the Lakers were swept out of the conference semifinals last season and underwent an out-of-nowhere ownership change in August. Another potentially major hang-up: The Lakers entered training camp with two unclaimed spots in their starting lineup.

While Doncic and guard Austin Reaves have an excellent bond, the Lakers clearly trail behind most of the leading title favorites when it comes to continuity. But from a talent and fit perspective, the Lakers can claim some resemblance to the 2023-24 Mavericks now that center Walker Kessler is in place. Doncic led that Dallas team to 50 wins and a surprise trip to the Finals.

Memphis Grizzlies

The preseason revealed ... Zach Edey is still a force

With Ja Morant, Jaren Jackson Jr. and Desmond Bane all departing the Grizzlies in separate trades since June 2025, it's easy to forget that Memphis has welcomed back a major talent as it ramps up for a rebuilding campaign. Edey, a 7-foot-3 center who played only 11 games last season before undergoing season-ending ankle surgery, has returned to claim his spot as the Grizzlies' starting center. In Friday's exhibition win over the Bulls, Edey made his presence felt with 10 points and five rebounds in just 16 minutes.

The 2024 lottery pick has the size and strength to control the glass and punish small-ball lineups in the paint, but Memphis must use this season to craft a sustainable role for him given his immense frame and history of lower-body injuries. Despite its roster overhaul, Memphis has assembled a solid frontcourt rotation that also includes Rookie of the Year contender Cameron Boozer and bruising backup center Isaiah Stewart. If Edey can put his injury woes behind him -- a big if -- the Grizzlies should be competing for a spot in the play-in tournament before too long.

Miami Heat

The preseason revealed ... Giannis Antetokounmpo made a good first impression

It will take months to get used to seeing Antetokounmpo in a Heat jersey after his 13-year run with the Milwaukee Bucks, but so far No. 7 in white has looked a lot like No. 34 in green on the court. Antetokounmpo pummeled the New Orleans Pelicans in a recent exhibition, blasting through a crowded paint for punishing dunks, racing ahead in transition to aid Miami's preferred up-tempo approach and making the proper reads after drawing multiple defenders.

Given how much time Antetokounmpo missed due to injuries last season and the career-altering trade that shaped his summer, the two-time MVP is off to a promising start with the Heat. Offseason concerns about Miami's 3-point shooting acumen haven't really materialized in the preseason, though it's fair to question whether the Heat have enough talent beyond Antetokounmpo and Bam Adebayo to keep pace with the East's best.

Milwaukee Bucks

The preseason revealed ... the veterans will get first dibs

Many teams mix and match their starting lineups during the preseason to test various configurations or rest veterans, but new Bucks coach Taylor Jenkins has made sure his most accomplished players have been on the floor together. That makes sense: It will take time for the post-Antetokounmpo Bucks to mesh their holdover pieces with a batch of former Heat players who arrived in this summer's blockbuster.

Milwaukee appears ready to enter the season with Ryan Rollins, Tyler Herro, Jaime Jaquez Jr., Kyle Kuzma and Myles Turner as its starting five, a group that will likely struggle to reach league average on offense and defense. As the season unfolds, Jenkins must decide when to prioritize the development of younger players such as Kel'el Ware and 2026 lottery picks Brayden Burries and Nate Ament. While that possible shift could be aided by unloading players at the trade deadline, the balance of present and future won't be influenced by draft positioning -- the Bucks have already traded away their 2027 first-round pick.

Minnesota Timberwolves

The preseason revealed ... the vibes are looser

Timberwolves coach Chris Finch recently summarized his team's new identity in succinct fashion: "We've traded moodiness for giddiness." That checks out, given that Minnesota spent the summer pairing Anthony Edwards with LaMelo Ball in a charismatic Zoomer backcourt and moving on from Julius Randle and Naz Reid. Throw in forward Jonathan Kuminga, who was signed in free agency, and the Timberwolves have seemingly transformed from "Edwards and a bunch of veterans" to "Rudy Gobert and a bunch of young guys."

But Finch surely understands that Minnesota faces serious competition in the West's playoff bracket. The initial giddiness that comes with any honeymoon period must eventually be complemented by resolve and maturity. The Timberwolves' offense should be more fun and less predictable with Ball in the mix, but discipline and focus in high-pressure moments loom as hurdles.

New Orleans Pelicans

The preseason revealed ... the prospects are taking a back seat

The Pelicans' roster-building strategy has been puzzling. After winning just 26 games last season, are they trying to squeeze better results from a mediocre roster or are they ready to start building the future? Jamahl Mosley, hired as coach in May, appears to be leaning toward competitiveness rather than development.

Mosley opened the preseason with a veteran-dominated starting lineup featuring Zion Williamson, Dejounte Murray, Trey Murphy III, Herbert Jones and Yves Missi. In turn, 2025 lottery picks Jeremiah Fears and Derik Queen both came off the bench. While Fears, 19, and Queen, 21, combined for 97 starts last season, both struggled to score efficiently as rookies and now must start over with their second coach in two seasons. The Pelicans are a team to watch in the run-up to the trade deadline: If the wins don't materialize in a meaningful way, the right move would be to hand over more responsibilities to the youngsters.

New York Knicks

The preseason revealed ... James Dolan isn't afraid to be the villain

The NBA's parity era has been brutal on defending champions. Each of the past eight have lost key players, encountered untimely injuries, or simply run out of gas in attempts to defend their titles. The pace of modern basketball makes it nearly impossible for teams to hold up for 100-plus games in consecutive seasons, and the current collective bargaining agreement's onerous apron penalties are always lurking, ready to break up juggernauts.

Knicks owner James Dolan has taken an unsentimental approach to those harsh realities: His desire to avoid the second apron led to backup center Mitchell Robinson's offseason departure, and the Knicks' recent statement that they have paused negotiation talks with Karl-Anthony Towns and Josh Hart wasn't exactly welcome news. "Very disappointed to say the least," Towns said this week. If New York follows recent precedent and falters in its title defense, Dolan has set himself up to be viewed as the billionaire bogeyman who let money ruin his organization's rare moment in the sun.

Oklahoma City Thunder
The preseason revealed ... Aday Mara is found gold

Mara struggled to make a positive impact when surrounded by fringe talent in the unstructured confines of the Las Vegas summer league, but the enormous Spanish center has hit the ground running with the loaded Thunder in the preseason. It already feels unfair that Oklahoma City landed him with the 12th pick in June's draft: During a standout exhibition against the Bucks, Mara finished lobs, tossed backdoor passes, left Kel'el Ware grasping at air with spin moves in the post and made all 10 of his field goal attempts. For fans of a certain generation who prize deft footwork from big men, Mara is a gift that will keep on giving all season.

The Thunder clearly concluded they needed more interior size after their Western Conference finals loss to Victor Wembanyama's San Antonio Spurs, and the 7-foot-2 Mara will make it easier for coach Mark Daigneault to manage the 82-game slog. There should be minutes available because starting center Isaiah Hartenstein has missed 37% of Oklahoma City's games over the past two seasons, and Mara has enough offensive skill and versatility to function alongside any of the Thunder's other big men.

Orlando Magic

The preseason revealed ... Tristan da Silva is launching

It's always worth monitoring which role players benefit or suffer when a new coach arrives. In Orlando, da Silva has been reaping the rewards of first-time head coach Sean Sweeney's emphasis on spacing and ball movement. Though da Silva averaged a modest 3.7 3-point attempts during his first two seasons with the Magic, the 2024 first-round pick launched 10.7 treys per game in his first three preseason appearances.

For context, only Stephen Curry, Luka Doncic and LaMelo Ball attempted more than 10 per game last season, and no player in Magic history has averaged more than 7.7. Empowering da Silva makes sense for Sweeney given that Paolo Banchero and Franz Wagner are inconsistent outside shooters; Orlando's star forwards should theoretically become more efficient offensive weapons with more room inside the arc.

Philadelphia 76ers

The preseason revealed ... LeBron James' latest superteam is pacing itself

The veteran-laden 76ers haven't exactly raced out of the gate: In Philadelphia's first three exhibition games, James took a total of one shot and logged only 18 minutes while coach Nick Nurse rotated 10 players into his starting lineups. Given James' age (41) and Joel Embiid's injury history (extensive), the Sixers are obviously more focused on April, May and June than October and November.

Don't be surprised if Philadelphia's slow feel-out period continues into the regular season. James has a history of rough beginnings when he changes teams: The 2010-11 Heat started 9-8, the 2014-15 Cavaliers started 5-7 and the 2018-19 Lakers started 4-6. Of course, Miami and Cleveland went on to reach the NBA Finals, so it's probably best to reserve judgment on the 76ers until at least Thanksgiving.

Phoenix Suns
The preseason revealed ... Khaman Maluach is coming along

The Suns project as a low-ceiling team that won't generate much excitement beyond Arizona's borders: Devin Booker and Jalen Green form a fine backcourt pairing, but they don't exactly put a scare into the elite teams in the West. If Phoenix can escape the play-in tournament as it did in 2025-26, that will qualify as a successful season. The exception to its ho-hum vibe is Maluach, a 20-year-old center who barely played as a rookie last season.

The 7-foot-1 Maluach was bigger, stronger and better than the Las Vegas summer league competition in July, and he built on that showing with a well-rounded performance against Victor Wembanyama's Spurs on Saturday. Maluach is more than just a dunker and a shot blocker: Against San Antonio, he fed a cutter from the high post, stepped out to hit a 3-pointer and came up with a steal while trapping outside the arc. The Suns should be able to give their 2025 lottery pick plenty of developmental minutes as they wait for starting center Mark Williams to return from September shoulder surgery.

Portland Trail Blazers

The preseason revealed ... Ja Morant should come off the bench

Damian Lillard's early returns represent some good news for the Blazers, who endured a brutal summer marked by stalled arena negotiations and a botched broadcasting hire. Despite sitting out last season because of an Achilles injury, the 36-year-old star has generally looked sharp and shot the ball well in exhibition action. Though Portland should still be careful with his early-season ramp-up, Lillard's readiness brings much-needed clarity to a guard-heavy roster.

The best way for new coach Micah Nori to balance his lineups is to play Lillard alongside Scoot Henderson or Jrue Holiday then move Morant -- a surprising summer trade acquisition -- to the bench. Morant has been less impressive in the preseason, and Nori should not feel obligated to defer to his star power. Shifting Morant to the second unit also would benefit Deni Avdija, who should be treated as the centerpiece of this refashioned roster.

Sacramento Kings
The preseason revealed ... Maxime Raynaud dodged a bullet

Though not exactly a household name, the 2025 second-round pick was a bright spot during the Kings' miserable 2025-26 season. Raynaud averaged 12.5 points and 7.5 rebounds to earn second-team All-Rookie honors, establishing himself as a rare hit for an organization with a checkered draft history.

The Kings appear headed for another dismal season after losing their first four exhibition games, but they caught a break when Raynaud apparently avoided a serious right knee injury in a loss to the Warriors on Saturday. After exiting the court in a wheel chair, the 23-year-old French center was diagnosed with a patellar subluxation that will force him to sit out the season opener but should allow him to return relatively soon. Given Sacramento's roster is short on young talent to grow with 2026 lottery pick Darius Acuff Jr., a more serious injury for Raynaud would have been a crushing blow.

San Antonio Spurs

The preseason revealed ... San Antonio is close to answering to its biggest question

No team is facing a more consequential lineup decision than the Spurs, who must decide whether to make room for 2025 No. 2 pick Dylan Harper in a starting lineup that has included guards De'Aaron Fox, Stephon Castle and Devin Vassell. Though San Antonio's decision will shape its internal chemistry, the 2027 title race and Harper's ascent, the reigning Western Conference champions haven't officially tipped their hand. With Fox sitting out the Spurs' first three preseason games, the lineup debate has raged on in his absence.

The Spurs don't have much on-court evidence to go on because Fox, Castle and Harper shared the court for only 25 minutes during the 2025-26 regular season. Victor Wembanyama's singular defensive presence nullifies most of the usual concerns about conceding size with a three- or four-guard lineup, but coach Mitch Johnson does still need a high-level playmaker to lead his second unit. When push comes to shove, San Antonio should bet on Harper's potential, move Vassell to the bench, start Tobias Harris at power forward and give the three-guard lineup an extended test drive. To make that plan work, Johnson must creatively stagger his rotations to ensure that either Fox or Harper is always on the court.

Toronto Raptors
The preseason revealed ... Kawhi Leonard is ready to turn the page

Understandably, Leonard never had much to say about the NBA's yearlong investigation of the Clippers' role in salary cap circumvention. Even after the punishments were doled out and he was officially traded to the Raptors, Leonard sidestepped the issue at a September news conference by saying that he wanted to "move forward and focus on my time being a Toronto Raptor."

The best way for Leonard to actually turn the page is to play at an All-NBA level and lead Toronto to meaningful playoff success. The two-time Finals MVP got off to a great start on that front during his preseason debut Tuesday, torching the undermanned Knicks for 21 points in only 17 minutes. Raptors coach Darko Rajakovic should be thrilled to finally have a certified alpha scorer; no Toronto player has averaged 25 points since Leonard departed for the Clippers in 2019.

Utah Jazz
The preseason revealed ... the offense should be light years better

Utah has a strong case to be the NBA's most improved team from a watchability standpoint. Though that statement says something about how miserable the Jazz's defense was during their 22-win season in 2025-26, it also hints at the significant potential of this season's upgraded offense.

Lauri Markkanen, Jaren Jackson Jr. and Keyonte George are all proven high-level scorers, and 2026 No. 2 pick Darryn Peterson should be at or near the top of his class in points per game. Importantly, the Jazz's whole should be greater than the sum of its parts because their most important players are all effective floor spacers and willing passers. After ranking 22nd in offensive efficiency last season, Utah could jump 10 spots if it gets a Rookie of the Year-worthy season from Peterson plus good health for Markkanen and Jackson.

Washington Wizards
The preseason revealed ... Trae Young's pass-first pledge looks real

When Young met with reporters in July after signing a four-year, $212 million extension, he made it clear that his primary responsibility was to keep the Wizards' many scoring options involved in the offense. Young suggested he would be taking a more pass-first approach to get the most out of a roster that features 10-time All-Star Anthony Davis, 2026 No. 1 pick AJ Dybantsa, 2024 No. 2 pick Alex Sarr, 2025 No. 6 pick Tre Johnson and Kyshawn George, among other capable scorers.

Sure enough, Young dished 23 assists and attempted only 16 shots through Washington's first three preseason games. That's quite the extreme makeover for a four-time All-Star guard who has averaged 18.3 shots during his eight-year career, but radical measures are in order after the Wizards ranked 29th in offensive efficiency and 28th in assist-to-turnover ratio last season.

stories.headline: The UFC's flyweights are hot again - is Lone'er Kavanagh the next star?
stories.summary: Could a breakout win at UFC 333 propel Britain's Lone'er Kavanagh into the flyweight title picture?
stories.body:
The fighting life of a UFC flyweight was once an unenvied one.

Constant uncertainty over the future of the division, a lack of big pay-per-view interest and an unfortunate routine of far too many fighters getting cut for the weight class to sustain itself were just some of the problems that characterised the modern era. UFC president Dana White put it in simple terms, saying after Demetrious Johnson's UFC exit in 2018 that "people didn't care" about the flyweights. Even Olympic gold medalist and former two-division champion Henry Cejudo struggled to see how the flyweight division would continue as a part of the UFC, with his own brash persona and entertaining title defences pivotal to maintaining awareness of the division.

Much has changed since the days of Cejudo though, and the flyweights now have a genuine claim to being one of the most exciting divisions in the whole of the UFC. And one man at the forefront of that charge is another promising fighting talent from across the Atlantic, with England's Lone'er Kavanagh enjoying a rise like few others this past year.

He accepted a short-notice fight against ex-champion Brandon Moreno in the lion's den of Mexico City in March and produced one of the most stunning UFC upsets in recent memory, taking the unanimous decision win in front of a hostile crowd. Kavanagh was unranked before that fight and despite more recently losing to Brandon Royval at UFC 329, he remains just a win away from breaking into the flyweight title conversation. Taking on Royval on the night of Conor McGregor's return in Las Vegas in July, Kavanagh was submitted but earned the fight of the night on one of the promotion's most-watched recent cards in a back-and-forth slugfest. The 27-year-old's exciting style and high ceiling was on show that evening and will be again when he faces Ramazonbek Temirov on what is remarkably just his second high-profile numbered event at UFC 333 on Oct. 24.

"Thinking back to certain moments [in Mexico City], it was like a rollercoaster, it was a sick opportunity and I'm glad I did it and my team backed me to do it," Kavanagh tells ESPN.

"[Royval was] another step on the journey, losing is never fun, no matter what stage you're at whether you're at the top or at any point of your career but unfortunately sometimes you have to learn like that -- learning on the go, that's what we're doing right now.

"I believe I've got the best team around me so I truly believe with this team I can make it all the way to the top and that's the plan, that's the aim.

"I'm always trying to work on things from every fight. Unfortunately, you learn a lot more when you lose."

For Kavanagh, the lights have quickly turned brighter. Like many of his British counterparts in the UFC, he was made in Cage Warriors, the organisation that can take credit for the likes of McGregor, Paddy Pimblett and Tom Aspinall. From there, a first round knockout on Dana White's Contender Series saw the journey in the big time begin. His first professional defeat came in the UFC against the experienced Charles Johnson, but that was quickly forgotten with the Moreno heist that saw his stock in the game skyrocket. Kavanagh's front-footed, devious style stemming from his kickboxing roots has even earned him praise from one of the greatest to ever step in the octagon with a Jon Jones Facetime after that UFC Mexico win leaving him "starstruck."

"Your Muay Thai is beautiful, your kicks, they don't show at all. They have no telegraph. It's so nice," Jones said to Kavanagh.

It is a style that was born at London's Great Britain Top Team (GBTT), where alongside UFC veteran Nathaniel Wood and fellow prospect Shanelle Dyer, Kavanagh has honed his craft, going from a five-time K1 kickboxing champion to now potentially a statement win away from challenging for UFC gold under British MMA trailblazer Brad Pickett. And that too in a division where the competition is possibly as fierce as it has ever been. Royval, Tatsuro Tairo, Manuel Kape, Asu Almabayev and bona fide flyweight royalty Alexandre Pantoja make up the spine of a group of challengers that Kananagh finds himself a part of.

Joshua Van's UFC 331 title defence ended any doubts about his validity as champion, with a dominant win over Pantoja, and at just 24-years-old he looks set for a stint at the top -- where Kavanagh aspires to be. But first, No. 7 ranked, one below Kavanagh, and unbeaten in the UFC, the explosive Temirov is one of the toughest challenges the Englishman has faced in his career, and in a weight class as deep as the flyweights, back-to-back losses would see Kavanagh fall mercilessly down the pecking order -- the stakes are high at UFC 333.

"I think the flyweight division is the best division at the moment. It's forever changing," Kavanagh says. "There are so many young up and comers but there are also so many people that have been around for so long. So it's got a good mixture of everything and to be honest, just excited to be a part of it - it's sick being a flyweight at this time.

"I'm a very 'one fight at a time' kind of person, I'll always look at what's in front of me and then what's next but I think it would be an exciting fight either way, [Joshua] Van vs. Lon."

Born in London to an Irish father and Chinese mother, Kavanagh wears his heritage on his sleeve with his name Lone'er translating to "Little Dragon" in English. He credits his mum for pushing him into MMA, a decision that has since paid dividends.

Kavanagh is now set to be a part of a main card alongside two title fights at the Etihad Arena in Abu Dhabi. In his way, Uzbekistan's Temirov is coming in red hot on the back of a first-round finish against Steve Erceg, he last tasted defeat in an MMA bout seven years ago and has never been knocked out.

"I haven't seen all the fighters just fighting like me. Just striking punches, just making knockouts. But my punches will just kill them all," Temirov told the UFC.

The kickboxer is aware of the danger that Temirov carries but also the opportunity up for grabs.

"I think a win there puts me right back up there. He's a dangerous opponent. He's got some good wins under him, a lot of wins, but I think a win against him puts me right back up at the top. [I'm] always looking for a finish," Kavanagh said.

"His main weapons are his heavy hands, and that excites me. I love fights like that and I think it's a good fight for me. Hopefully [another fight of the night], I'm looking for more performances of the night."

As is now customary with Kavanagh's UFC bouts, his throwdown against the formidable Temirov is one not to be missed. With the top of the flyweight division so deep he will want to turn all the excitement surrounding him into consistency to earn a shot at Van's belt, that journey will take its latest step in a treacherous division.

And as Bruce Buffer introduces both fighters, perhaps there will be something for the UFC bosses and fans alike to take away before a single punch is even thrown. That all these years after Cejudo and Johnson have been and gone, the flyweights are box office property once again.

stories.headline: Dembélé jokes he might ask for more holidays after PSG's win at Man City
stories.summary: Ousmane Dembélé joked he might ask coach Luis Enrique for more time off after starring in PSG's 4-2 win at Manchester City in the Champions League.
stories.body:
Ousmane Dembélé joked he might ask coach Luis Enrique for more time off after starring in Paris Saint-Germain's 4-2 win at Manchester City in the Champions League.

The Ballon d'Or winner scored one goal and assisted on another in Wednesday's game. Luis Enrique had rested him after the recent international break, allowing Dembélé to sit out Saturday's home game against Le Mans, and he looked razor-sharp against City.

"After the international break I went on holiday. Actually, I might ask for more holidays," Dembélé told broadcaster Canal Plus. "I really enjoy playing on Tuesday and Wednesday, especially when I come back from holiday. It's a real pleasure."

Asked if he would go on holiday again, a smiling Dembélé added: "It's possible, until March I think. It's the coach who decides."

PSG have a trip to Strasbourg in Ligue 1 on Saturday, ahead of another high-profile Champions League game at home to Lamine Yamal's free-scoring Barcelona next Tuesday.

Luis Enrique may again rest players. He also omitted left-back Nuno Mendes against Le Mans, while Dembélé sat out a game against Lille in Ligue 1 earlier this season.

Dembélé won the French league's best player award last season, despite starting only nine games in PSG's title-winning campaign. The decision to award him the trophy over other players who played significantly more games led to criticism.

City coach Enzo Maresca said PSG enjoy a luxury his team and other Premier League sides don't have, being able to rotate players against modest Ligue 1 sides.

"They can manage players when they play games before the Champions League," he said. "For us, it's a bit different, especially when you go [to] Anfield."

City played Premier League rival Liverpool in a heated atmosphere on Sunday, giving Maresca's side one day less to prepare for the PSG game.

Last season, the French league accepted PSG's request to postpone their game against title rival Lens to allow better preparation for a Champions League quarterfinal against Liverpool -- a decision perceived by some observers as preferential treatment.

PSG went on to win the trophy for a second straight year, beating Arsenal on penalties in the final.

Dembélé has scored three Champions League goals, but has not yet found the net in four Ligue 1 matches this season. PSG are in sixth place after six rounds and some performances have fallen below expectations.

"We couldn't care less that people doubted us. We're in October, it's only the second game of the Champions League," he said. "We just need to stay on track during the first half of the season and prepare for the second."

However, he acknowledged PSG's concentration dropped off against City.

"We eased up a bit in the second half," Dembélé said. "When you do that against players like that, you pay for it."

stories.headline: Ferrari protege Rafael Câmara completes Haas driver line-up for F1 2027
stories.summary: Brazilian sensation Rafael Câmara will replace Esteban Ocon at Haas in 2027, the team confirmed on Thursday.
stories.body:
Brazilian sensation Rafael Câmara will replace Esteban Ocon at Haas in 2027, the team confirmed on Thursday.

Câmara, 21, the reigning Formula 3 champion and current Formula 2 leader, has joined on a multiyear deal. He will partner fellow Ferrari Driver Academy member Oliver Bearman at the team next season.

Haas had already confirmed Ocon will leave at the end of the year -- the one-time F1 race winner has yet to find his next move.

Câmara's signing sets up a fascinating situation at the Ferrari partner team -- Bearman has long been seen as the next in line to replace Lewis Hamilton whenever he moves on, but Câmara's arrival will likely force the narrative that it's an ongoing audition for that seat should the opportunity arise.

Câmara paid tribute to Haas and Ferrari, who signed him to their programme in 2021, for the move.

"I'm very happy to be joining Haas as a Formula 1 driver," said Câmara. "It's an important step in my career and I want to thank Gene Haas and Ayao Komatsu for the trust they have placed in me.

"I'm also very grateful to the Scuderia Ferrari Driver Academy for their support and for everything they have contributed to my development over the years, as well as to my family for always being there throughout this journey. Now my focus is on preparing myself in the best possible way for this new challenge. There will be a lot to learn, and I'm looking forward to working closely with the team, understanding the car and continuing to develop as a driver."

Câmara has already tested for Haas, with the team giving him mileage in the 2025 car under the Testing of Previous Car (TPC) rules at Portugal's Portimao circuit in August.

Former Alpine driver Jack Doohan, McLaren reserve Leonardo Fornaroli and Toyota-backed Ryo Hirakawa were all given opportunities to test for Haas as well, but sources have told ESPN Camara emerged as the clear favourite in terms of pace.

The youngster will have several opportunities to participate in Friday practice for the team between now and the end of the year, including his home race in Brazil at the start of November.

For Haas, it's the chance to sign another highly promising young driver to their roster.

Komatsu said Câmara especially impressed during the Portimao test.

- 'Chucky' Verstappen is back. Luckily for Antonelli and Mercedes, it's too late

- Formula 1 to return to Africa in 'early 2030s' as Rwanda race confirmed

"I'm really excited to sign such a young, amazing talent like Rafael Câmara," said Ayao Komatsu, Team Principal of TGR Haas F1 Team. "I don't need to tell everyone about his achievements in the junior formulas, it's been very impressive, and in his rookie season in Formula 2, the speed he's shown in some very difficult moments, like qualifying in Monaco and Montreal - that all goes to show the potential Rafa has.

"He showed when we had him drive in our TPC program in Portugal that he could handle himself very well with not a huge amount of time to learn the car, he showed us more than just raw speed. Rafa managed to create an environment to get the best out of himself, it was very impressive and certainly the laps he completed were special.

"We're all excited about this opportunity and really committed as TGR Haas F1 Team to nurture this talent and provide a place where he can flourish. We want to create an environment where he's comfortable and supported, where he can really excel in his capabilities."

The move will only bolster Haas' partnership with Ferrari, which has existed since the American team's F1 debut in 2016.

Team owner Gene Haas added: "I'm excited to see what Rafael Câmara can achieve in Formula 1 having seen his accomplishments coming up through the ranks in Formula 3 and now Formula 2 this year. It's a different challenge at this level but what we've experienced through Ollie Bearman following a similar trajectory and association with the Scuderia Ferrari Driver Academy, these younger drivers are well prepared, and they can make an immediate impact on a team.

"Rafa impressed the team with his TPC performance, so we look forward to building on that and growing our relationship full-time next season."

stories.headline: Wysh List: The NHL team being run by a fan
stories.summary: Sunny Mehta is a former derivatives trader and poker player and AGM of the Panthers -- but grew up rooting for the Devils.
stories.body:
NEWARK, NJ -- "Do you still think I shouldn't be the general manager of this team?"

I'm sitting in a lounge at the Prudential Center across from Sunny Mehta, who was hired as the general manager of the New Jersey Devils, despite my apparent protestations. I didn't recall holding this particular opinion, but a quick search revealed a podcast interview where I fully endorsed his candidacy for the team's vacancy -- provided he had an experienced executive working above him with the Devils.

"I wouldn't want him to, like, run the whole show," I said at the time.

And now Sunny Mehta is running the whole show ... and taking some measure of satisfaction watching me squirm while singed by my own hot take.

I've known Sunny for a bit now. His first podcast interview was on the old "ESPN On Ice" show with me and Emily Kaplan. I should have known this gotcha moment was coming, because when you sit down at a table with Sunny Mehta you assume he's going to be systematically prepared in ways that you are not.

Mehta, 48, is the latest in a wave of NHL general managers with roots in the analytics movement and taking nontraditional paths to their front office jobs. Eric Tulsky, the movement's standard-bearer, built a Stanley Cup winner in Carolina 20 years after analyzing the synthesis of cadmium-free nanocrystals for clinical applications as a scientist for a nanotech company in Washington state.

Like Tulsky, Mehta has an untypical background. While other current GMs were inhaling Zamboni fumes at the rink, Mehta was a derivatives trader in Chicago and a professional poker player, having authored two books on card-playing strategy. Like Tulsky, he entered the NHL first as a data consultant and then as an analytics director, before becoming an assistant general manager. Mehta won the Stanley Cup twice in that capacity with the Florida Panthers before replacing Tom Fitzgerald as Devils general manager this year.

But he also shares something else with Tulsky: He's a hockey fan living the dream. Tulsky first caught the hockey bug as a commenter on Philadelphia Flyers blogs. Mehta is a lifelong Devils fan who now runs the Devils. The kind of kid who would rock a red-and-black Starter jacket while sitting in the Meadowlands stands, cheering on someone nicknamed "The Little Ball of Hate."

As a young Devils fan, Mehta loved Pat Verbeek, and still remembers the exhilaration of his 46-goal season in 1987-88, then a Devils record. Verbeek went from NHL player to NHL general manager. Mehta went from NHL fan to Verbeek's peer.

"I remember talking to Verbeek when I was an AGM in Florida about that 46-goal season. He was like, 'I f---ing got hurt at the end. I would've had more!' It was really funny," Mehta said. "I obviously talk to Pat in a different capacity now, but I still kind of break his balls about it."

Verbeek played 1,424 games in the NHL. He's one of 13 current general managers that have played at least 500 NHL games. Other managers are longtime player agents (Bill Zito, Kent Hughes), descendants of hockey royalty (Stan Bowman, Chris Patrick) or have worked in NHL front offices since the 1990s (Don Waddell, Ken Holland).

Was there ever any concern for Mehta that these hockey lifers might not talk to him the way they talk to each other? He acknowledged it's been an apprehension for others. "Maybe even owners, at certain points," he said.

But Mehta said he was never concerned, personally.

"I think the thing that people forget is when you're the GM, people have to call you because they want your players. They want to trade with you. It'd be stupid for them to not call you. It'd be stupid for them to not try to get along with you, to not be nice to you," he said. "Agents are looking for your money, so they want you to sign their players. It was super easy to forge a ton of new friendships and relationships."

While working for the Panthers, Mehta had a window into the interactions between GMs and agents. He took part in trade discussions, but now gets to engage in trade negotiations. Which made me curious: How does a former poker pro read opponents when trying to win a trade?

"I think the poker part of it is more the pre-negotiation part, thinking through all the probability and the strategy. But when I first started talking to other GMs, I was probably the least 'poker' in the sense that I just called guys and I was like, 'Here's who I like.' I kind of just think being transparent and trying to be as direct as possible is a better policy than trying to be too clever and bluffing," he said. "Instead of treating them as an adversary, treat them as a partner. You're going to get more bees with honey than vinegar, you know what I mean?"

There's also a strategy in managing internal relationships. Despite his affinity for the team, Mehta is an outsider to these Devils. He has history with some players -- forward Evan Rodrigues, for example, who was acquired from Florida when Mehta flipped goalie Jacob Markstrom to the Panthers -- but not the majority. He enters a situation with some complicated power dynamics behind the scenes, coupled with a lack of playoff success on the ice.

What's it like being a new general manager trying to understand those dynamics?

"Oh God, what's that show?" asked Mehta. "The second season took place in Italy. It had Stiffler's mom in it."

HBO's "The White Lotus," perhaps?

"Yeah. 'White Lotus,'" he said.

"I only watched the first season, but I felt like that was a show where there's literally no good guys and no bad guys. Every character is kind of flawed, but also has some endearing qualities," Mehta said. "It's a weird analogy, but instead of looking at [the team] in terms of who the good guys are and who I can trust, you just think about how every party has their own perspective. No one's the good guy. No one's wrong. Just hear everybody out, hear all sides of the story. The truth is somewhere in between."

On "White Lotus," you eventually find out who the murderer is.

"But there's no murderer!" he said of the Devils. "That's what I'm saying. There is no murderer."

After gathering information on his new team, Mehta made three quick decisions. He traded disgruntled restricted free agent defenseman Simon Nemec -- the No. 2 overall pick in 2022 -- to Calgary. He vowed to the veterans on his roster with trade protection that he'd honor it, a list that included 33-year-old defenseman Dougie Hamilton, who has a full no-movement clause, two more seasons at $9 million against the cap and saw his name swirl in trade rumors under Fitzgerald.

"I do have a lot of respect for Dougie's game. I hope he crushes it this year," Mehta said.

His most significant decision was trading Markstrom, the team's starting goaltender for the last two seasons. That left the Devils in the hands of Jake Allen and Nico Daws, a cost-efficient but uninspiring tandem that left fans wondering if, yet again, the team would be subverted by its goaltending.

Mehta's approach to his netminding was, perhaps, his most scrutinized philosophy so far as general manager. He made waves in an NHL.com interview when he said, "I'm reluctant to invest significant assets there instead of in areas where the results may be more predictable."

Mehta didn't quite understand the pushback.

"I think a lot of opinions I've expressed about goaltending are turned into single quote memes or headlines. 'Oh, he doesn't care about goaltending' or something like that," he said. Mehta said that's a misconception. It's just that it's a position marinated in uncertainty in comparison to others.

"Even if we went out and got whoever you think is the best goaltender, the probability of that person actually performing as the best goaltender results-wise next year is far lower than if you took a bet on, say, whether Connor McDavid going to be in the top five in scoring. There's way higher probability of that bet being right than any bet on goaltending," Mehta said.

It's hard to know what hand Mehta is playing right now until the final card is revealed: The one with Quinn Hughes on it. The defenseman wants to play with his brothers Jack and Luke, who want to play with him. Quinn has yet to sign a contract extension with the Minnesota Wild and is an unrestricted free agent next summer. The Devils are, of course, mentioned frequently while the mystery builds.

Is Mehta keeping his powder dry for a run at Quinn Hughes if the Wild don't lock him down, either via trade or free agency?

"As I've said all along, I don't want to comment on any player on another team. I'm just always looking for good players at good prices. So whether it's Quinn or any high-end player around the league ... I guess what I'm saying is, to some extent, when I make that decision, I almost have to ignore people's last names," Mehta said.

"My job is to win a Cup. My job is to freaking put a winning team on the ice. Whatever it takes. However [long] it takes."

Like Mehta, I grew up a Devils fan. My fandom remains an inherent part of my hockey DNA, passed onto my children. We watch this sport because we love this sport, and to suppress the origins of that love is counterintuitive to connecting with one's audience.

And so I'll be honest about this, too: Sunny Mehta is living the dream. Not just for a kid who sat in the nosebleeds at Brendan Byrne Arena like we both did, but for any hockey fan that has at one point convinced themselves that they could build a Stanley Cup winner if only given the chance, because they did it on a video game or because their message board trade proposals are that sick.

He's one of us. He didn't play 1,000 NHL games. He's not a hockey nepo baby. He's a guy who waxes poetic about the magic of Alex Mogilny, the guy who felt a jolt of nostalgia when he saw Pat Verbeek talking with Scott Niedermayer at the NHL Draft Combine one day.

"I just walked up to them and I was like, '30 years ago, this would've been a dream for me, you guys,'" he said.

Guys like Mehta and Tulsky are fantastic for the game because they gives fans a chance to live vicariously through one of their own -- even if we're not poker aces or nanotech scientists, which are the points of differentiation between us and these geniuses.

We're fans. They're fans. And Mehta takes personal responsibility for delivering a Stanley Cup to his people for the first time since 2003.

"That's the goal. It's the dream. Every day I wake up still and I'm pinching myself. I can't see ever taking this role for granted because of how much it means to me," he said, nodding his head towards me.

"You understand, right?"

I do. As hockey fans, I think we all do.
